articles.title: Nepal: Rescuers battle treacherous terrain, shortages to find missing
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On Friday afternoon, an Armed Police Force rescue team reached the wreckage of a security post in Timure, a remote settlement in Rasuwa bordering China. The rescuers were searching…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On Friday afternoon, an Armed Police Force rescue team reached the wreckage of a security post in Timure, a remote settlement in Rasuwa bordering China.
The rescuers were searching through the debris left by Wednesday’s devastating flood when one of them heard something unexpected: a child crying.

“At the surface, nothing was visible,” said APF Deputy Inspector General Netra Bahadur Karki. “We suspected someone was trapped beneath the debris. The team immediately began digging through the collapsed structure and successfully pulled a six-year-old girl out alive.”

The team belonged to the APF’s Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue unit, created in 2011 for major disasters. It has 285 trained personnel equipped to cut through concrete, steel and timber in difficult terrain. Members are also trained in combat medical care.
The girl was stabilised at the scene and taken to the Border Outpost in Timure. Bad weather prevented her immediate evacuation to hospitals in Dhunche or Bidur.
Her rescue was one of many taking place across the flood zone as Nepal’s security forces race against time to find people still trapped, missing or cut off.

The APF has deployed 4,203 personnel in specialist teams, including search-and-rescue dog squads, diving teams, rope rescuers, medical units, drone operators and personnel managing temporary holding centres.
“Our dog squads are locating five to seven bodies daily based on scent cues,” Karki said.

The disaster struck at about 8:40 am on Wednesday, when a huge surge swept down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, destroying roads, bridges, settlements and other infrastructure across central Nepal.
Seven Nepali Army helicopters and eight private aircraft have since been flying rescue and relief missions.
Among those deployed are troops from the Army’s elite Ranger Battalion. On Friday, they rescued four workers trapped inside an intake tunnel at Rasuwa Hydropower Project.
The tunnel entrance had been buried under thick slurry and the surrounding terrain was so badly altered that rescuers could not immediately locate it.

“The entire land structure had shifted; there was no visual landmark left to identify the entrance,” said Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, the Army spokesperson, who is coordinating military operations from the Bidur barracks.
Army officers worked with project engineers and used structural plans to determine the tunnel’s location. Military engineers then used specialised equipment to break through the obstruction.
Images from the rescue show workers crawling towards the light through thick mud as soldiers moved in to extract them.

Rescuers lowered a heavy basket from a hovering helicopter and, secured by harnesses, crawled through the mud to reach the trapped men. The four survivors were then lifted out and flown to Kathmandu for treatment.
The operation illustrates the central problem facing rescue teams: in many places, the flood has not simply blocked access but erased the landscape itself.

Across the river basin, 84 frontline officers from the Army, Nepal Police and APF are involved in high-risk searches. In total, 4,811 Nepal Police personnel have been deployed for rescue, body recovery and logistics.
By 3:30 pm on Saturday, security forces had recovered 669 bodies from eight districts downstream, according to Senior Superintendent Abi Narayan Kafle, the police spokesperson.
Police commanders have positioned retrieval teams along the river corridor from Rasuwa to the southern plains, using drones to scan riverbanks and debris fields.
When sensors detect human remains beneath wreckage or sediment, ground teams equipped with hydraulic cutters and other power tools move in.
Once a body is recovered, it is tagged, placed in an airtight body bag and taken to a designated hospital.
Authorities record photographs and distinguishing features and, when necessary, collect fingerprints and biological samples for identification.

The scale of the disaster is already overwhelming those systems. Police say nearly 2,000 people have been reported missing by relatives in Makwanpur, Dhading, Kavre, Sindhupalchok, Dolakha, Ramechhap, Sindhuli, Chitwan and Nuwakot, while figures for Rasuwa were still being compiled.

“Given the sheer volume of casualties, storing bodies indefinitely is impossible,” a senior police field commander said. Authorities are therefore preparing emergency procedures for DNA sampling, fingerprinting, detailed records and tagged burials.
Home Minister Sudan Gurung has said the immediate priority is to save lives.
“Our security personnel are working without sleep,” Gurung said. “Until a missing person’s body is found, our operational assumption is that they are still alive and awaiting rescue.”
Helicopters have become the main lifeline for communities cut off by destroyed roads and bridges.

blocks.caption: Nepali Army personnel rescue people trapped inside a hydropower project tunnel in Rasuwa following the Bhotekoshi flood. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

blocks.text: At the Army Barracks in Battar, Bidur, and at the Dhunche helipad, aircraft are taking off and landing continuously. Outside the razor-wire perimeter in Bidur, families wait and watch every incoming helicopter.
On Friday, Gurung went to speak to them. The meeting quickly heated up as angry relatives questioned the government over warnings and the speed of the rescue response.
“If the administration had alerted us the moment the surge crossed the northern border, the entire bazaar could have been evacuated in time,” one resident shouted through the fence.
Gurung defended the crews operating in narrow mountain valleys in dangerous weather. He cited the tunnel rescue as evidence that teams were reaching trapped victims.
Among those waiting was Nani Chaulagain, whose relatives remain trapped near the Trishuli Hydropower complex while her injured husband is being treated in Kathmandu.
“I don’t even have the money to travel to Kathmandu to be with my husband,” she said. “My family members are still stuck up there, and nobody can tell us when the helicopters will reach them.”

Police estimates suggest that about 100 people remain stranded around Timure. Preliminary reports also put the number unaccounted for at around 200 near the Mailung Upper Trishuli-A site, another 200 in Syaphrubesi and Haku, at least 50 at Tiru Secondary School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-1 and 10 at the Save the Children compound in Biruwadanda.
Yet police face a basic limitation: they have no aircraft of their own.

“We have highly trained disaster response personnel on the ground, but because the Nepal Police owns no aircraft, we cannot deploy our units independently,” a senior police officer said. “In many remote sectors, our officers can only move when paired with Nepali Army helicopter missions.”

A police inspector in Rasuwa said emergency calls to the hotline number at 100 continue to come from stranded villagers, but ground teams often cannot reach them because roads have been destroyed and air transport is limited.
The disaster has revived a long-running debate over whether Nepal Police should have its own aviation capability.

Former Inspector General of Police Achyut Krishna Kharel wrote in his 2018 autobiography about repeated difficulties securing helicopter support during the Maoist conflict in the 90s. Proposals for police helicopters were submitted in 1996 and 1997, and a purchase was approved by the government in 2000 before the decision was reversed.
Successive police chiefs, including Rabindra Pratap Shah, Kuber Singh Rana, Sarbendra Khanal and Dhiraj Pratap Singh, later renewed calls for dedicated aviation assets.
“The lack of dedicated air assets for the police remains a critical bottleneck,” Singh said.
The APF faces the same problem. A senior officer said the force had repeatedly sought light helicopters for disaster response, but the proposals had not been approved.
The need for specialised equipment is equally pressing.

Nepali Army’s former Colonel Ratindra Khatri, a disaster management specialist, said the first 72 hours after a disaster are the most critical for locating survivors, although people can survive much longer in exceptional circumstances.

“Statistically, the vast majority of life-saving extractions occur within the first 72 hours,” Khatri said. “That initial window closed on Saturday morning, meaning operations must maintain absolute, maximum intensity.”
As the window narrows, rescuers are also battling severe shortages of equipment.
Police teams in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan initially held 765 body bags and had used 194 by Saturday. Another 77 were being requisitioned from unaffected districts.
Field teams have also reported shortages of chainsaws, power tools and heavy-duty cutting equipment needed to clear trees, structures and debris.
Nepal has expanded the response by bringing in Nepal Red Cross volunteers and military recruits undergoing basic training for logistics and distribution work.

The government has also begun relying on specialised international assistance. After initially saying domestic forces had sufficient capacity, authorities later coordinated with India for a team of tunnel rescue specialists as the complexity of underground rescues became clearer.
Former Additional Inspector General of Police Thule Rai, who specialises in disaster logistics, said the scale of the destruction required sustained deployments across the entire river corridor.

“We need maximum boots on the ground,” Rai said. “Because the Trishuli river corridor is devastated, from the high border passes all the way to the southern plains, small deployments are ineffective.”
He said rescuers also needed advanced technical skills because unstable riverbanks and damaged structures posed serious risks to rescue teams themselves.

Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said specialised equipment capable of detecting survivors beneath mud and collapsed structures could significantly improve operations.

“When I headed the authority, we attempted to procure these systems, but faced acute global supply shortages,” Pokhrel said. “Securing such equipment now will not only aid current operations but build long-term national resilience.”

By 8 pm on Saturday, the NDRRMA said 7,514 people had been rescued or otherwise assisted nationwide. The authority said 191 people had been pulled from flooded hydropower tunnels, 517 stranded people had been airlifted on Friday alone and 717 foreign tourists had been evacuated from high-altitude trekking routes.
For military commanders, however, the priority remains the same: find those who may still be alive.
“Ranger units are deployed across virtually every accessible sector in Rasuwa,” Basnet said. “Our primary focus remains on search and rescue for the living, rather than body recovery.” /dl

articles.title: DSWD brings in 24,029 food packs to Ilocos Region amid rains
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has delivered 24,029 family food packs (FFPs) to various warehouses and prepositioning areas in the Ilocos Region…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has delivered 24,029 family food packs (FFPs) to various warehouses and prepositioning areas in the Ilocos Region as it prepares for possible relief operations amid continuing rains.

Three trucks carrying 5,179 FFPs arrived on Saturday, Aug. 29, at the DSWD Field Office 1 satellite warehouse in Laoag City, Ilocos Norte, while another truck delivered 1,700 FFPs to a prepositioning area in Vigan City, Ilocos Sur.
The deliveries were part of the agency’s continuing replenishment of relief supplies and efforts to ensure that food packs are readily available for families who may need assistance as rains persist.
Additional FFPs were also delivered to the DSWD regional warehouse in Biday, San Fernando City, La Union.
The DSWD said the additional stocks would strengthen its capacity to respond to communities that may be affected by prolonged rainfall, flooding and other weather-related incidents in the region.

The agency continues to coordinate with local government units and disaster response authorities to ensure the timely distribution of assistance to affected families. — Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor /das

articles.title: [Tambay] Kaya ba ng mga kooperatiba na maghalal ng senador?
articles.summary: Pangako ng mga lider sa harap ng Coop Vote hindi sila pipili ng sikat o artista, dahil ang mahalaga ay may puso sa cooperative principles

blocks.text: Sa 2028 pa ang pambansang halalan, pero noong Biyernes ng tanghali eleksyon na ang usapan sa isang hotel sa Maynila. At hindi mapigil ng pagbabalik ng habagat yung mainit na kuwentuhan ng mga taong matatayog ang pangarap.
Pabiro pa nga silang binansagan ng tambay na ito na “dreamers” dahil nga sa tayog ng inaambisyon nila.

Bahagi ng National Leadership Congress ng Philippine Chamber of Cooperatives (Coop Chamber) na ginanap nung maulan na Biyernes na iyon ay isang press briefing. Sa briefer inanúnsiyó ng Coop Chamber ambisyosong bagong project nila. Ito ang Senatorial Project / Coop Vote.
Sa madaling salita magpapatakbo ang Coop Chamber ng sarili nilang kandidato o mga kandidato para sa Senado.

Bakit ko tinawag na ambisyoso? Kasi hindi ito simpleng endorso ng kandidato. Hindi rin ito pagpapatakbo ng partylist sa House of Representatives. Kasi mayroón ng mga kinatawan ang ilang sector-based groups. At ang kadalasan pókus ng mga ito ay ang kailangan ng kanilang sector. At dahil nga kakarampót ang bilang ng mga grupong coop-based sa Kamara, hindi matutukan ang mga mas malalawak na pangangailangan ng mga kooperatiba sa Pilipinas.

Ang inaasinta ng Coop Vote ay magpatakbo ng sarili nilang kandidato para sa Senado. Hindi lang endorso, kundi mismong kandidato. At kung masusunod ang kanilang balákin, bubuo na din sila ng Coop Party.

Aaminin na ng tambay na ito na malapit sa kanyang pusò ang cooperativism. Noong kasibulan ng kanyang paninilbihan sa Philippine Daily Inquirer (kung saan lagpas 30 taon siya nagtrabaho), bumuo sila ng multi-purpose cooperative para sa mga empleyado. Patawarin ninyo na ang flex na ito, natulungan ng Inquirer Coop ang karamihan ng empleyado, mula sa simpleng kawani hanggang sa top executives.
Kaya buo ang aking suporta sa mga pagkílos palakasín ang mga cooperative sa bansa.

“Panahon na para kumilos ang mga kooperatiba. Hindi na nanonood lang sa mga nangyayari sa ating bansa… The Senatorial Project and the Coop Vote are not merely political exercises, they are a structural awakening. By organizing primary cooperatives across all 16 regions into a disciplined, proactive legislative bloc, we are making it clear that no national policy, budget, or reform will be forged without honoring the voices and livelihoods of our millions of member-owners,” sabi ni Edwin Bustillos, secretary general ng Coop Chamber.
Totoo ang numerong nabanggit niya.

Sabi sa cooperatives.com: “The Philippines has one of Southeast Asia’s most developed cooperative sectors, with over 27,000 cooperatives registered with the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA) and more than 16 million members — approximately 15% of the population. The sector spans agriculture, savings and credit, consumer goods, transport, and housing, making it a cornerstone of rural economic development.”
Ang Cooperative Development Authority ang sangay ng gobyernong nangagasiwa sa mga coop sa bansa. Ang Coop Chamber naman ay samahan ng mga kooperatiba na nagtutulungan.
Maraming consultation na gagawin ang Coop Chamber, pero desidído silang ito ang landas na dapat nilang tahakin, sabi ni Noel Raboy, chair ng Coop Chamber.

Pero ang umantig sa puso ko ay yung sinabi ni Marlene Sindayen, Coop Chamber vice chair at trustee. Kapag matuloy na ang pagtakbo ng kandidato ng mga coop, mag-aambag ng limang piso ang bawat isang coop member para suportahan ang kampanya nila. “Maliit na halaga lang yan. Pero ipapakita namin na kami ang magbibigay o mag-aambag ng pera at hindi tatanggap. Ipapakita namin na hindi kami nabibili.”

Ang totoo niyan, kakapirasong halaga ang limang piso. Pandagdag lang. Pero ito ang naglalarawan sa karaniwang kasapi ng mga coop — mga ordinaryong Pilipino na paunti-unting inaangat ang buhay sa konting kíta, konting ípon. Mga namamaluktot muna habang untî-untî nilang mapalaki ang maikling kumot.
Sabi ni Noel, isa o hanggang tatlong kandidato sa senado muna ang kanilang patatakbuhin sa pambansang eleksyon sa 2028.

Nabanggit din niya na ang inspirasyon ng Coop Chamber ay si Andy Burnham, ang bagong prime minister ng United Kingdom. Si Burnham ay miyembro ng Co-operative Party na ka-alyansa ng Labour Party na nagluklok sa kanya maging punong ehekutibo.
Nung marinig ko ito, naisip ko: aba, teka, puwedeng mangyari din yan dito sa Pilipinas.

At ang mariin na pinangako ni Noel, “hindi kami pipili ng politiko. Hindi kami pipili ng artista. Hindi dahil din sikat, patatakbuhin namin. Ang gusto namin naniniwala at sumusunod sa mga prinsipyo ng cooperativism.”
Parang may nais tumbukín si Noel?
Pero teka bakit itong senador na namang ito ang pumasok sa isip ko.

Ipinangako na kasi ng tambay na ito sa kanyang saríli na lumubay muna sa pagpuna at komentaryo sa mga kabulastugan ni Senador Robinhood Padilla tuwing impeachment hearing ni Vice President Sara Duterte sa Senado.

Sa palagay ng tambay na ito ay marami pang may kabuluhan na pampalipas oras ang mapagkukuwentuhan. At malamang ay wala nang magagawa ang senador para lalo pang maibaon ang sarili sa kumunoy ng kapurulan.
Pero nagkamali ako. Pinatunayan na naman ng topnotcher senador ang katangian niyang sana ay nakikita na rin ng nakararami.

Nung impeachment hearing kasi nung nakalipas na linggo binulalas ni Senator Robin ang mga nom de guerre at nom de plume ng mga bayaning rebolusyonaryong nag-aklas noong panahon ng himagsikan. Ang pinupunto niya ay walang mali sa paggamit ng alyas.

Inihalintulad niya ang mga alias ng mga dakilang bayani kanila Mary Grace Piattos at iba pang alias sa mga acknowledgement receipts na tumanggap diumano ng bayad galing sa confidential funds ni VP Sara. Mga alias din daw dahil nagbigay sila ng intelligence information at dahil diyan dapat ikubli ang kanilang tunay na identity.
Hindi pinakinggan ni Padilla ang paliwanag ng abogada ng prosekusyon na “non-issue” ang usapan sa alias dahil hindi naman ito inireklamo sa impeachment.
Ang punchline pa ni Senator Robin ay nung tinanong ang abogada: kilala mo ba si Marcial Bonifacio? At sa tono pa ng pagtatanong ni Padilla, parang siya lang ang nakakaalam ng sagot.
Maraming komentarista ang hindi maubos maisip bakit si Ninoy Aquino pa ang napili ni Padilla na gawing punchline ng kanyang interjection. Wala namang kinalaman ang bayani sa confidential funds.

Usapan paggamit din lang naman ng mga alias, kilala ba ni Robin si William Saunders and Jane Ryan? Iyan ang alias nila Ferdinand at Imelda Marcos noong nagbukas sila noong 1968 ng mga Swiss bank accounts.

Ok, sige lumapit na tayo sa mundong kinagisnan ni Senator Padilla. Bakit hindi siya humugot sa mundo ng showbiz? Halimbawa: Kagalang-galang na senador, kilala po ba ninyo si BB Gandhari? – Rappler.com
Si Chito de la Vega ay Tambay ng Rappler dalawang beses kada buwan. Kasama rin siya sa mga anchor-host ng programang Balita Kwento Serbisyo ng DZME 1530.

articles.title: CHR calls for end to impunity, censorship on National Press Freedom Day
articles.summary: The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) urged the government Sunday to address impunity and promote safe civic spaces free from censorship and intimidation as the country celebrates National Press…

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 10:56am

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) urged the government Sunday to address impunity and promote safe civic spaces free from censorship and intimidation as the country celebrates National Press Freedom Day.
In a statement, CHR said a free and independent press is vital to democracy, empowering communities, holding power accountable, and amplifying the voices of marginalized and disadvantaged sectors.
“When journalists are silenced, people lose information necessary to make informed decisions, participate meaningfully in public life, and hold institutions accountable,” the CHR said.
“A free press is essential to a society where human rights are respected, violations are exposed, and people can demand accountability,” it added.
The Commission also called for swift justice for victims of red-tagging and other forms of threats to journalists and their families.
World Press Freedom Index
The Philippines ranked 114th in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, up slightly from 116th the previous year.

Despite the improvement, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) noted that the Philippines remains one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists, ranking in the bottom half of the 180-country index.
“Protecting journalists must therefore extend beyond physical safety to addressing intimidation and vilification that restrict press freedom,” CHR said.
In August 2025, CHR and the Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFoMS) signed a memorandum of agreement to improve services aimed at protecting media workers.
The agreement provides concrete actions that will lay out real protections, prompt response, and justice for media workers in distress, particularly those who face harassment, threats, and violence.
The CHR also conducted regional consultations to strengthen its Framework on Media Welfare and Human Rights and Philippine Plan of Action on the Safety of Journalists.
Through the commission’s Alisto! Alert Mechanism, media workers may also directly report threats and incidents for appropriate monitoring, investigation, and response.
CHR reiterated its support for the decriminalization of libel and cyberlibel and urged Congress to replace imprisonment with proportionate civil remedies.

The Commission also called for the review of both versions of the proposed Digital Media Anti-False Information Act and for the adoption of a human rights-based approach that protects legitimate expression and press freedom while addressing the roots of disinformation.
The Digital Media Anti-False Information Act is a proposed measure that imposes prison terms and fines of up to P2 million on those found guilty of willfully spreading false information.
The CHR further sought to protect journalists’ data, communications, and sources while ensuring that responses to emerging technologies uphold human rights.
On April 13, 2022, former president Rodrigo Duterte declared August 30 National Press Freedom Day in honor of Marcelo H. del Pilar, the father of Philippine Journalism. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Iceland EU referendum sees slim, early lead for 'yes' camp
articles.summary: The 'yes' camp won 51.2% of the vote in early counting, but election officials stressed that a more reliable result might not be ready until later on Sunday.

image.caption: Members of the 'yes' campaign welcomed early resultsImage: Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Early results from Iceland's referendum on resuming European Union membership talks showed a slim lead for the "yes" camp on Sunday night.
With 87,00 ballots counted, 51.2% of ​voters were in favor of the government's ​proposal to resume EU negotiations, while 48.8% opposed it, Iceland's public broadcaster RUV reported.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.
Election officials warned that a more reliable result might not be available until midday on Sunday.
Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc's 28th member. Talks were suspended 13 years ago by the euroskeptic government at the time.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
This article will be updated as votes continue to be counted in Iceland.

articles.title: 4-day break unwinds Bukidnon
articles.summary: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Residents across Bukidnon are enjoying a rare four-day long weekend that bridges the usual Saturday-Sunday-Monday rest period straight into Tuesday, diverting from the…

blocks.text: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Residents across Bukidnon are enjoying a rare four-day long weekend that bridges the usual Saturday-Sunday-Monday rest period straight into Tuesday, diverting from the standard resumption of work and classes.

With Aug. 31 observed as a regular holiday in the Philippines for National Heroes Day, and the province observing a special non-working holiday known as “Araw ng Bukidnon” on Sept. 1 in commemoration of its foundation anniversary, locals have taken full advantage of the extended pause to unwind.
Common activities filling the long weekend include sleeping in late, spending quality time with family, and diving into personal hobbies and recreational interests.
Republic Act No. 12039 permanently establishes Sept. 1 as a special non-working holiday across the province, celebrating the 112th founding anniversary of “Araw ng Bukidnon.”
The key activities for the anniversary celebrations include a night market open daily from 5 p.m. onwards, featuring local food trucks, street food, seafood stalls, and various other merchants.
There will be a live concert featuring a popular Manila artist on Sept. 1, starting at 6 p.m. at the capitol grounds.
There are also sports events, including the Bukidnon Softball Baseball Confederation games, Bukidnon Moto Festival, and the Panagtigi Pickleball Tournament.

A socio-civic parade along the national highway in Malaybalay City and a flag-raising ceremony will be held on Sept. 1 at the capitol grounds to commemorate the milestone history of the province while showcasing and honoring its rich cultural heritage.
Bukidnon has a rich history rooted in its indigenous mountain tribes and the Spanish and American colonial eras.
The name “Bukidnon” comes from ”bukid,” the Tagalog and Visayan word for mountain, meaning “mountain people” or “highlanders.”
Its history showed that on Aug. 20, 1907, the Philippine Commission enacted Act No. 1693, organizing Bukidnon as a sub-province of Agusan, with Malaybalay designated as the capital. /das

articles.title: Nepal flood survivors face second crisis as medicines, water run short
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — For Rekha Devi Gosain, surviving the flood was only the first ordeal. The Trishuli Bazaar resident lives with diabetes, high blood pressure and thyroid disease, conditions that…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — For Rekha Devi Gosain, surviving the flood was only the first ordeal.

The Trishuli Bazaar resident lives with diabetes, high blood pressure and thyroid disease, conditions that require regular medication. When the flood swept away her home and four shops she owned, there was no time to save her medicines. Her vehicle, motorcycle and other belongings were also lost.
Now she and her family are living in a displaced-persons camp near Trishuli Hospital. But the hospital does not have the medicines she needs.
“My mother has to take her medicines regularly, but the hospital does not have them,” her son Raghubir said. “It has been three days since she was able to take them.”

The family’s ordeal did not end there. Raghubir’s sister-in-law went into labour while sheltering at the camp. Trishuli Hospital could not handle the delivery, but the family had no road access to Kathmandu.
After repeated appeals, she was airlifted on Saturday morning to the Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital in Thapathali, Kathmandu, he said.
The same shortage is affecting many other displaced people. Patients with chronic illnesses have gone many days without medicines after losing their homes and belongings.
At Kolani, another displacement camp, Kopila Pariyar is caring for her 62-year-old mother, who has asthma and depends on regular medication.
“My mother has asthma and needs two or three medicines, but we have not been able to get all of them,” she said.
The family is also struggling to find basic necessities.
“There is no drinking water in the camp and we cannot even buy bottled water. We have no money, no clothes and there is almost nothing to buy in the Kolani market,” Pariyar said.
Her 16-year-old brother Abinash and 43-year-old sister-in-law Shanti are among those missing after the flood.
Doctors warn that people with chronic conditions should not be forced to stop taking essential medicines. Yet Trishuli Hospital itself is running short.
Hospital pharmacist Maheshwar Yadav said medicines commonly prescribed for hypertension, including atenolol and losartan, were unavailable.
“Our hospital insurance programme is also not operating because there is no internet, and we are running out of medicines,” Yadav said.

Rikesh Rana, information officer at Trishuli Hospital, said many displaced people sheltering nearby have diabetes, high blood pressure and asthma but are unable to obtain the medicines they normally take.
The shortages extend beyond drugs.

The flood has cut the main sources of drinking water to the hospital and surrounding settlements. Residents and the hospital had previously drawn water from a canal serving the Trishuli hydropower project, but the flood destroyed the canal. A separate water pipeline bringing supplies through Tupche was also washed away.
With both systems gone, displaced people and local residents are being forced to use whatever water they can find.
Doctors fear the water shortage and poor sanitation could trigger a second disaster: disease outbreaks in crowded camps.

Three displacement camps have been established in the Baghtaar area around Trishuli Hospital. About 1,000 people are staying at Bhairung Secondary School, the covered hall and Bethan Academy. Among them are pregnant women, new mothers and people needing medical care.
Clean water and sanitation are in short supply, while poor drainage from toilets is adding to the concern.

“With so many people living together in one place, there is a risk of disease spreading,” said Rajendra Lama, medical superintendent of Trishuli Hospital. “The lack of safe drinking water and proper toilets raises the possibility of an epidemic.”
Displaced residents also complain that the food being provided at the camps is inadequate and lacks sufficient nutrition, a particular concern for pregnant women, new mothers and those who are ill.
The destruction of every bridge in the area has also severed the hospital’s connection with the district headquarters, making it difficult to move patients in or out.
Lama said helicopters are not always available when patients need urgent evacuation.
“The bigger problem is bringing pregnant women to the hospital and taking them home,” he said. “If we need to refer a patient, there is no option other than evacuation by helicopter.”
The hospital is now struggling to keep its own operations going.
Essential medicines are running low. Cooking gas is unavailable. Ambulances are running short of diesel.
And the security situation is deteriorating.
Lama said only seven or eight police officers were currently deployed around the hospital and nearby areas, leaving residents and medical staff increasingly vulnerable.
“Looting has started during the day itself. We need more police patrols and security,” he said.
On Friday, four or five masked men arrived on motorcycles and reportedly drove away doctors who were carrying out an operation, Lama said. Looting has since begun at houses in the surrounding area.
“There was looting in broad daylight on Friday,” he said.
The disruption has also fuelled black-market activity, making it difficult to obtain basic goods, Lama said. /dl

articles.title: Child rescued from hostage-taker in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur— Police rescued a minor who was held hostage in Barangay Daddaay, Alilem, Ilocos Sur, on Saturday, Aug. 29. The Ilocos Sur Police Provincial Office (ISPPO) said the suspect,…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur— Police rescued a minor who was held hostage in Barangay Daddaay, Alilem, Ilocos Sur, on Saturday, Aug. 29.

The Ilocos Sur Police Provincial Office (ISPPO) said the suspect, a 37-year-old man reportedly with a mental disability, was inside a house with the child when police arrived after receiving a report about the incident.
Personnel of the Alilem Municipal Police Station immediately responded and began negotiating with the suspect in an effort to safely resolve the situation.
While negotiations were underway, a concerned resident called out the suspect’s name, prompting him to look toward a window.
Police seized the opportunity to move in and pull the child away from the suspect, successfully rescuing the minor.
The child, whose age was not disclosed, sustained wounds to both legs and was given first aid by a rural health unit nurse who was at the scene.
According to investigators, the victim was later brought to the Ilocos Sur District Hospital-Bio in Tagudin for further medical attention.
The suspect’s relationship to the victim was not immediately known.
Police said the operation was carried out with caution to protect both the child and the suspect and prevent further harm. — Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor /das

articles.title: Nepal to preserve DNA before burial of unidentified flood victims
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday that the government would preserve DNA samples and other identifying evidence from bodies that cannot be identified before taking steps…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday that the government would preserve DNA samples and other identifying evidence from bodies that cannot be identified before taking steps to bury or otherwise manage them.

In a statement posted on social media on Saturday evening, Shah said only unidentified bodies would be handled by the government, while those identified by their families were being handed over to relatives.

“Only bodies that cannot be identified will be managed by the government after preserving DNA and other evidence that could help establish their identity,” he said. He urged the public not to be misled over the government’s handling of the dead.
Prime Minister Shah said that 675 bodies had been recovered so far from different locations in Rasuwa, Dhading, Nuwakot, Chitwan, Tanahun, Gorkha, Nawalparasi East and Nawalparasi West.
The recovered bodies are being placed in airtight bags and managed under the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management (First Amendment) Directive, 2026, he said.

The devastating flood that struck the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on August 26 caused extensive loss of life and damage to property and infrastructure along the river corridor, including in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Shah said the government had intensified search, rescue, treatment, relief and communications restoration operations immediately after the disaster.
The response is being carried out in coordination with federal, provincial and local authorities, he said, with government agencies working at full capacity to protect those affected.
“Saving the lives of every affected citizen remains the government’s first priority,” Shah said.
He said the government would remain alongside affected communities and continue rescue and rehabilitation efforts until tangible results are achieved. /dl

articles.title: Army’s 10ID honors 4 former commanders in rare camp homecoming
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Four retired military generals who once steered the Army’s 10th Infantry Division (10ID) returned to their former headquarters on Friday, Aug. 28, in a rare homecoming…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Four retired military generals who once steered the Army’s 10th Infantry Division (10ID) returned to their former headquarters on Friday, Aug. 28, in a rare homecoming tribute honoring the leaders who shaped the unit’s operational legacy.

Held at Camp General Manuel T. Yan Sr. in Barangay Tuboran, Mawab, Davao de Oro, the “Agila Tribute” was organized by Maj. Gen. Alvin Luzon, 10ID commander, to recognize retired Gen. Noel Clement, retired Gen. Jose Faustino Jr., retired Lt. Gen. Ernesto Torres Jr., and retired Maj. Gen. Reuben Basiao.

Clement and Faustino both rose to become the 52nd and 56th chiefs of staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, respectively. Torres later headed the Northern Luzon Command and served as executive director of the NTF-ELCAC National Secretariat.

During the gathering, the honorees reflected on their leadership journeys at the helm of the division and expressed gratitude to Luzon for the opportunity to reconnect with former colleagues and personnel.
“Your names are part of our history. Your accomplishments are part of our institutional memory. Your lessons continue to influence the way we lead and serve,” Luzon told the former commanders.

Luzon also challenged the current roster of troops to protect and advance the gains of their predecessors as the division transitions from sustaining an insurgency-free jurisdiction to posturing for external security operations.
“To the current leaders and personnel of the Agila Division, this homecoming should remind us of our responsibility. We have inherited a legacy, something we must strengthen,” Luzon said.
The event featured a ceremonial toast and the presentation of “The Eagle” paintings to each honoree.
Also in attendance were retired Assistant Division Commanders Brig. Gen. Mario Lacurom and Brig. Gen. Maning Tawantawan, alongside other former senior officers of the 10ID. /das

articles.title: Oriental Mindoro grid has 29.34-MW power reserve — TransCo
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Oriental Mindoro power grid had a 29.34-megawatt (MW) power reserve as of 6 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 30, according to the latest dispatch report from the National…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Oriental Mindoro power grid had a 29.34-megawatt (MW) power reserve as of 6 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 30, according to the latest dispatch report from the National Transmission Corp. (TransCo)-Mindoro Control Center.
The grid had a total dependable capacity of 71.41 MW against the province’s electricity demand of 42.07 MW, leaving a reserve margin of 29.34 MW.
An additional 3.04 MW of spinning and regulating reserve was available to help maintain grid balance and stability.
The total contracted capacity from new power providers (NPPs) in Oriental Mindoro was listed at 100.50 MW, indicating sufficient contracted supply to meet the province’s long-term requirements.
Power plants with active generation included DPC at 8.31 MW, DPC Lot 1 at 5 MW, IMHPP at 10 MW and OPI at 7.43 MW, among others.
Several facilities, however, recorded low or zero output during the monitoring period, including Topteam Calapan, SPC Socorro, TPI Calapan and Regulus Puerto Galera.

The POC CDPP plant reported no generation due to fuel supply constraints, while some generating units were being used for voltage support and to prevent overloading of the transformer at the Socorro Substation.

TransCo’s dispatch report showed that the Oriental Mindoro grid had sufficient reserve capacity to meet current demand, with no immediate indication of a need for rotational brownouts due to a supply shortfall.

Oriental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (Ormeco) General Manager Engr. Humphrey Dolor attributed the available reserve partly to lower electricity demand among member-consumers and increased generation from hydroelectric plants.

“The low production of some IPPs (independent power producers) is due to the delay in the release of the UCME (Universal Charge for Missionary Electrification) from the National Power Corp. (NPC), which is allocated for fuel purchases,” Dolor said in a message Sunday.
Dolor said the reserve situation should be viewed alongside the operating conditions of individual power producers, particularly those affected by fuel availability. /das

articles.title: Floods wipe out Nepal local governments’ ability to lead rescue, relief
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in the Bhotekoshi river, disaster management efforts in the severely affected Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have lurched into a deep crisis.…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in the Bhotekoshi river, disaster management efforts in the severely affected Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have lurched into a deep crisis.

Local governments—constitutionally mandated as the primary line of response during natural disasters—have themselves been overwhelmed and physically dismantled by the flooding, crippling rescue, relief, and data collection operations across the region.

In Gosaikunda Rural Municipality of Rasuwa, the vice-chair Pratima Tamang, two ward chairpersons and several employees are out of contact. According to chairman Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, seven members of his own family are also missing; the rural municipality office and two ward offices were washed away by the floods.

“My rural municipality has more than 2,000 people, including the vice-chair, two ward chiefs and seven members of my own family, who have gone missing in the flood,” Tamang told Kantipur. “The vice-chair has been out of contact since the flood and the search is continuing. How can we work in such a situation?”

Ward 5 chief Dawa Mingmar Tamang and ward 2 chair Kami Chhiring Tamang are among those missing, according to Gosaikunda’s executive member Pema Dorje Ghale. Ward 2 members Sonam Chhiring Ghale and Kami Shedar Ghale are also out of contact.
The vice-chair Pratima Tamang went out of contact from Syaphrubesi after the flood. The rural municipality’s ward 2 office in Timure and ward 5 office in Syaphrubesi were also swept away.

“Roads and electricity are gone, and telephone connections are difficult,” said chairman Tamang. “There is fear among residents, elected representatives and employees who are safe. Even so, we are trying as much as we can for rescue and relief.”

The August 26 flood has struck at the heart of the country’s disaster response system. Under the constitution, disaster management is both a local responsibility and a shared responsibility of the federal, provincial and local governments.

Local governments are also required by law to prepare disaster response plans, identify and map risk areas, coordinate search and rescue and relief, maintain disaster-related data and work with other levels of government and non-state actors.
But in the local units along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, the institutions responsible for those tasks have themselves become victims.

Krishna Bahadur BK, section officer in Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, said assistant accounts officer Kaisang Dindup Tamang, ward 2 secretary Prakash Acharya, employees Khambu Bohara, Kopila KC and agricultural technician Nar Bahadur Thapa, as well as office assistants Lakpa Tamang and Bishal Tamang, are out of contact.
With the main municipal building gone, the people’s representatives and officials are preparing to operate from Dhunche, the district headquarters of Rasuwa.

Engineer Jiban Bhatta said the immediate challenge was not only rescuing people but also reconstructing the basic machinery needed to provide relief. “Even the rural municipality’s letterhead and official stamp are gone. Collecting damage details, identifying people who need relief and carrying out administrative work have been severely affected,” he said.

The situation is even more stark in neighboring Uttargaya Rural Municipality, where the rural municipal office at Laharepauwa has disappeared along with the records stored inside. Vice-chair Chameli Gurung said the rural municipality building and the offices of wards 1 and 5 had been swept away.

“There is no telephone network and no electricity. We have no contact with anyone. We do not know who is where, and elected representatives and employees cannot contact one another. How can we work?” said Gurung. “You ask us for data. On what basis can we provide it? Please restore the telephone network and electricity first. Then we will collect the details.”

Gurung said preliminary information suggested that more than 1,000 people in Uttargaya Rural Municipality were out of contact. The loss of the municipal centre has also paralysed financial and administrative work, including allocating money for displaced people, collecting damage data and coordinating with wards. “When the municipal centre itself is gone, there is no way to carry out financial, administrative or management work,” said Gurung.

Jayaram Upreti, chief administrative officer of Uttargaya, survived after fleeing the flood, but five of his colleagues remain out of contact. He said they were caught while travelling in an ambulance to warn residents using a loudspeaker.

“While we were going around issuing the flood warning, our colleagues were caught in the flood at a place called Khalte,” said Upreti. With the office swept away, the municipality has no official documents, he said. “The employees are staying and working at the holding centers with the displaced people,” said Upreti.

The rural municipality is providing food and accommodation to around 750 people in four shelters. But the absence of roads and electricity has made it difficult to establish the scale of the damage. In some cases, parents remain missing while children have reached safety, leaving officials unable to establish complete family details.
The problem extends downstream into Nuwakot. Bidur Municipality has suffered damage in 10 wards. Municipal employee Subash Pandey said preliminary information showed 298 people out of contact.
Deputy Mayor Prabha Bogati said the municipality’s elected representatives and employees were safe and that officials were continuing to collect information on missing people.
Five motorable bridges in Bidur have been swept away, separating communities on either side of the Trishuli and making it difficult for families to reach one another.

“Until today, we focused on moving displaced people to safety and rescuing those who were stranded,” said Bogati. “The municipal disaster committee met on Friday and has started collecting details of the human and physical losses. Now we will prioritise relief and rehabilitation.”
She said the municipality had helped more than 100 students who had been unable to reach their families after a bridge was swept away to reunite with their parents.

The scale of the wider disaster has made the local governments’ predicament more serious. The Bhotekoshi flood struck Rasuwa on Wednesday morning and then moved downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, sweeping away homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure. By Saturday evening, police had reported 669 deaths across eight affected districts, with hundreds still missing.

Among the 15 local units declared disaster-hit by the government, Gosaikunda, Uttargaya and Kalika rural municipalities in Rasuwa, and Bidur and Belkotgadhi municipalities in Nuwakot, have suffered the heaviest human and physical losses.

The affected local governments said the damage had made it difficult to collect information on losses, arrange safe accommodation for displaced people and distribute relief. The disruption of roads, electricity and telephone services has further hampered coordination, they said.

The secretariat of Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives and Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal said 10 local-level employees, one rural municipality vice-chair, two ward chairpersons and two ward members were out of contact following the floods.

The Local Government Operation Act 2017 requires local governments to prepare disaster preparedness and response plans, identify and map areas at risk, take steps to protect and relocate vulnerable settlements, coordinate search, rescue and relief operations, maintain disaster-related data, and work with the federal and provincial governments, local communities, non-governmental organizations and the private sector.
With several local governments themselves severely impacted, the loss of personnel, records and basic infrastructure has made it harder for them to carry out these responsibilities.

Laxmi Pandey, chair of the National Federation of Rural Municipalities, said the federation was contacting representatives of affected municipalities and discussing how other local governments could help.

“The first priority should be to restore electricity and telephone services in the affected rural municipalities,” said Pandey. “Once communication is restored, it will be easier to contact them and provide support.”

Federalism expert Khimlal Devkota said the affected municipalities could not be expected to manage a disaster of this scale alone. “Federal and provincial governments, political parties and organizations all need to be involved,” he stressed. /dl

articles.title: Kiko Barzaga's mother wins Cavite 4th district congressional seat
articles.summary: Barzaga family keeps Cavite 4th District seat after Kiko's expulsion.

blocks.text: Newly-elected Rep. Jenny Austria-Barzaga
Jenny Austria-Barzaga via FB
MANILA, Philippines — The mother of expelled lawmaker Kiko Barzaga has won the special election for Cavite's 4th District held on Saturday, August 29.
Jennifer Austria-Barzaga garnered 201,893 votes, with voter turnout at 57.75%, according to Commission on Elections Chairman George Garcia.
The other candidates and their vote totals were:

items: Raul Rex Mangubat: 30,373
Jacinto Frani Jr.: 24,350
Marvin Dupal-Ag: 1,184
Leysander Ordenes: 561

blocks.text: Barzaga is the incumbent mayor of Dasmariñas City, Cavite.
She replaces her son, Kiko Barzaga, who was expelled from the House of Representatives on June 2, 2026.

The House expelled Barzaga for disorderly behavior and conduct unbecoming of a member following findings that he repeatedly disrupted plenary proceedings and violated House rules and ethical standards.

articles.title: LPA develops into tropical depression ‘Pilandok’
articles.summary: The low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) has developed into a tropical depression and was locally named “Pilandok,” the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and…

blocks.text: The low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) has developed into a tropical depression and was locally named “Pilandok,” the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Sunday, Aug. 30.

As of 8 a.m., Tropical Depression Pilandok was located 1,245 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon, with maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gustiness of up to 75 kph.
It was moving west-northwestward at 15 kph.
PAGASA weather specialist Obet Badrina earlier said PAGASA would continue to monitor how the weather disturbance interacts with the southwest monsoon or “habagat.”
For now, the habagat remains the weather system mainly affecting Luzon.

The rainfall outlook for Sunday showed that Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga could receive 100 to 200 millimeters or rain, considered heavy to intense.

Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro could receive 50 to 100 millimeters, or moderate to heavy rainfall.
On Monday, Aug. 31, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan.
Fifty to 100 millimeters could prevail over Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro.
By Tuesday, Sept. 1, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, Benguet, and Zambales.
Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Bataan, and Pampanga could receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall.
Despite the possible strengthening of the habagat, Badrina said rainfall over the western section of Luzon could decrease by Monday, Aug. 31, or Tuesday, Sept. 1.

blocks.text: Justin Arana has been activated for Gilas Pilipinas’ game against Iran in the fourth window of the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers at the Mall of Asia Arena on Sunday, Aug. 30.
The Converge big man is taking the spot of Carl Tamayo, who suffered an ankle injury in the Nationals’ 82-81 escape against Jordan in the first game of the window.
It marks the first time Arana will be playing for the national team after also being called up before the start of the team’s preparation in the window.
He will join Kai Sotto, June Mar Fajardo and AJ Edu at the frontlines with Justine Baltazar and Troy Rosario also patrolling the paint.
Kevin Quiambao, Dwight Ramos and Chris Newsome are filling up the wings while Scottie Thompson, CJ Perez and Juan Gomez de Liaño will man the point guard spot.
The Nationals will take on an Iranian team looking to bounce back from a tough 93-91 loss to New Zealand in the first game.

articles.title: DSWD taps volunteers to keep relief food pack stocks replenished
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is turning to volunteers to help replenish its supply of family food packs following the distribution of millions of relief packs to…

blocks.text: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is turning to volunteers to help replenish its supply of family food packs following the distribution of millions of relief packs to disaster-affected communities in recent weeks.

Volunteers are being welcomed at the Luzon Disaster Resource Center (LDRC) in Pasay City and the Visayas Disaster Resource Center (VDRC) in Mandaue City, Cebu, where repacking operations are conducted from Monday to Saturday.
DSWD National Resource and Logistics Management Bureau (NRLMB) officer-in-charge Director Jun Eso said the production hubs are open to volunteers from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

DSWD has been replenishing its family food pack inventory after millions of packs were distributed to families affected by the southwest monsoon or “habagat” and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng.
Before the habagat-enhanced rains, the department had reached its five-million family food packs prepositioning target, with the packs distributed among about 1,000 warehouses nationwide.

DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier directed the NRLMB to accelerate production and replenish stocks to the five-million target as part of efforts to ensure that relief supplies are readily available when disasters strike.

“Before po ng [bagyong] Luis, Maymay, at Neneng, we reached 5 million family food packs, and it’s a milestone for DSWD to have this strategically prepositioned all over the country. In case of any disaster, we could easily transport these family food packs to the affected communities (Before tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng, we reached five million family food packs, and it was a milestone for the DSWD to have these strategically prepositioned across the country. In case of any disaster, we could easily transport these family food packs to affected communities),” Eso said.
Eso said volunteers can help the department meet its daily repacking targets as it works to restore its inventory.
Interested individuals and groups are advised to coordinate with the NRLMB before visiting the facilities.
Walk-ins are allowed, but the DSWD is encouraging volunteers to register in advance to help organize shifts.
Volunteers must be at least 18 years old, while those below 18 must be accompanied by a guardian because heavy-duty machinery is used inside the warehouses.
They are also advised to wear appropriate clothing, particularly closed shoes, for safety.

“We would do brief orientation kung ano ’yung gagawin sa loob, and then at least 4 hours po [pwedeng] ma-render ng volunteer doon para ma-maximize din ’yung time natin while nandoon tayo kasi mayroon din tayong quota na niri-reach everyday (We would conduct a brief orientation on what volunteers will do inside, and volunteers may render at least four hours so we can maximize their time there because we also have a daily quota to meet),” Eso said.

articles.title: Haakon, the reluctant prince who became Norway’s new king
articles.summary: Over the years, Haakon grew into his role, becoming Crown Prince in 1991 and taking on more royal duties as his father's health failed. But it was a long and sometimes difficult adjustment.

blocks.text: NEW KING. Norway's then Crown Prince Haakon reacts as Norway wins in the cross-country skiing event at the Milano Cortina 2026 Olympics.
Kacper Pempel/REUTERS
Over the years, Haakon grew into his role, becoming Crown Prince in 1991 and taking on more royal duties as his father's health failed. But it was a long and sometimes difficult adjustment.

items: Crown Prince Haakon of Norway struggled with his royal identity during his childhood, preferring to stay out of the spotlight and choosing to study at the University of California, Berkeley, to distance himself from royal expectations.
He married Mette-Marit in 2001, who helped him come out of his shell, but their family faced scandals, including Mette-Marit's connection to Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius' legal troubles.
Haakon became Norway's fourth king in the modern era, expressing a newfound acceptance of his role and finding joy in his public position while valuing time spent with his family in the water.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
OSLO, Norway – Haakon — who comes to the throne as two major scandals batter his family — struggled for years to accept his status.
“Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it…. At school it made me anxious,” he wrote in his 2023 autobiography Haakon, recalling his days in a state primary in the 1980s.

Over the years, he grew into his role, becoming Crown Prince in 1991 and taking on more royal duties as his father’s health failed. On Friday, August 28, he took on the crown itself following the death of King Harald.
But it was a long and sometimes difficult adjustment.
As a child, he preferred to stay out of sight “because that is when things went wrong. Attention, other people could have that,” he wrote.

blocks.caption: Norway’s King Olav, Prince Haakon Magnus, and Crown Prince Harald, in front of Skaugum in Asker, Norway on September 17, 1982. Photo by Erik Thorberg/Reuters

blocks.text: He decided not to try to follow in his father and grandfather’s footsteps to England’s University of Oxford, and enrolled instead at the University of California, Berkeley.

He wanted to be “as far away as possible” from his home. Other attractions were California’s music scene — including one memorable, heavily policed concert by the Brooklyn-born rapper Nas in the middle of the East Coast-West Coast hip-hop rivalry.
And then there was the surf. “In the water, I could be myself,” he wrote.
Soon after his return to Norway in 1999 he met his future wife, Mette-Marit, at a music festival.
When the relationship became public, the media jumped on the fact that she was a commoner and a single mother who had spent a lot of time in her youth in Norway’s house music clubs.
That furor died down after King Harald — who had also married a commoner, Queen Sonja, despite his own father’s objections — publicly welcomed her into the family.

Haakon said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as the emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. “I am not very good socially,” he wrote. “Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone.”

blocks.caption: Crown Princess Mette-Marit of Norway and Crown Prince Haakon of Norway wave in celebration after Norway’s women’s handball team wins the gold medal in its match against France at the Paris 2024 Olympics on August 10, 2024. Photo by Bernadett Szabo/Reuters

blocks.text: They married in 2001 and had two children — Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, alongside Marius, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship.

More than two decades later, another media storm erupted when files published by the US Justice Department in January included email correspondence between Mette-Marit and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Mette-Marit did not respond publicly for seven weeks and Haakon released a statement saying his wife needed time to gather herself. When she did give a 20-minute interview to public broadcaster NRK in March, he was sitting by her side, saying marriage was both for “the good days and the bad.”
“Mette is caring, wise and really strong. And that’s why I will always have her on the team when something difficult happens,” the crown prince said.
At the same time the Epstein scandal was unfolding, Mette-Marit’s son Marius Borg Hoiby, Haakon’s stepson, was standing trial for rape and domestic violence, charges he denied.
Haakon issued a statement expressing sympathy with the alleged victims and saying he would not be in court.

“We support Marius in the situation he is in. We look after the other children as well,” he told reporters on the sidelines of a royal visit. “For me, the most important thing these past few days has been to take care of the flock.”

In June, Marius was found guilty of two out of four counts of rape and one count of domestic violence and sentenced to four years in prison. Both he and the prosecution have launched appeals against the sentence.

On Friday, Haakon became Norway’s fourth king in the modern era — which started when the country voted in a referendum to become a monarchy rather than a republic on declaring full independence from Sweden in 1905.
After that plebiscite, Prince Carl of Denmark became Norway’s King Haakon VII — building numerically on the line of Norwegian kings from the Viking and medieval eras.

The namesake and great-grandson of that monarch wrote in his autobiography that he had grown to embrace his public position. “I can find meaning and joy within it, and I can try and be of help to others.” If he keeps his name, he will become King Haakon VIII of Norway, though he can still choose to change it.
As for his private life, he said he still loved the water.

“As a grown-up, I am at my happiest in the water together with my family. It provides an inner peace when the flock is gathered to do what I like best: to be among the waves. Nothing beats that feeling.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PH expresses condolences to Norway on passing of King Harald V
articles.summary: The Philippines mourned Saturday with the people of Norway on the passing of King Harald V.

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 9:58am
The Philippines mourned Saturday with the people of Norway on the passing of King Harald V.
In a statement, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) described Harald as a source of “strength and inspiration” to the Norwegian people.

“For thirty-five years, King Harald V served as the "People's King,” who ushered progress, peace, and prosperity to Norway. His Majesty's legacy and memory shall remain as a source of strength and inspiration to the Norwegian people,” the DFA said.
“The Government of the Philippines conveys its sincere condolences to the Royal Family, the Government, and the people of Norway,” it added.

READ #DFAStatement — The Government of the Republic of the Philippines is deeply saddened by the passing of His Majesty King Harald V of the Kingdom of Norway.#DFAForgingAhead pic.twitter.com/bDCdka9PKO— DFA Philippines 🇵🇭 (@DFAPHL) August 29, 2026
Europe’s oldest monarch, Harald emerged from the shadow of his well-loved, extroverted father to become a reformer during more than three decades on the throne.
He died on Friday at the age of 89.

Flags were flying at half-mast throughout the country while portraits of the late king in gala uniform were everywhere, from bus stops, trams and metro stations to shops, offices and public buildings.
King Harald's son succeeded him at the throne.
In his first address, King Haakon VIII said his father was "such a good dad." —Mariel Celine Serquiña/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Australia could make social media algorithms optional and follow UK ban on pornography depicting strangulation
articles.summary: Social services minister says social media was playing a role in the increase of sexual violence among teenagers

blocks.text: The Australian government is considering allowing users to opt in or opt out of social media algorithms, and is looking at a recent UK ban on depictions of strangulation and suffocation in pornography.

The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said social media was “playing a huge role” in the increase in sexual violence among teenagers and choking, and confirmed the options were being considered as the government develops its second action plan to end family and domestic violence against women and children.

It follows the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney after a suspected sexual strangulation act. Guardian Australia reported on Thursday that a source informed about the case said the teenager was believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, often referred to as “choking”. No arrests have been made.
Plibersek told the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday that social media algorithms are deliberately feeding boys and men violent content and normalising strangulation during sex.

“If you set up a social media account as a young boy in Australia today, it takes an average of 23 minutes for you to be fed misogynistic, violent misogynistic content online. That is a deliberate decision of the social media companies that is wrecking our young boys, giving them all of the wrong ideas about what healthy relationships look like,” Plibersek said.

“It is no coincidence that 60% of young people now report that they’ve experienced strangulation during a sexual encounter … It is pervasive and widespread and deadly, and it’s being fed to our young people and normalised.”
Chanel Contos’s Teach Us Consent has campaigned for algorithms to be opt-in only on social media.
Plibersek said the government was working with the group and considering how to potentially design an opt-in or opt-out system for algorithms.
“We’re absolutely up for work on algorithms. Opting in to those recommender algorithms that are causing so much harm, opting in or opting out,” she said.

“We’re also, of course, looking very closely at the recent Meta case in the US [and] the moves that the UK government have introduced to prevent the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography. These are all really important considerations as we develop our next action plan on family domestic and sexual violence, so that work’s going on right now.”
after newsletter promotion

The government legislated a ban on social media for under-16s which took effect in December, and has also introduced age-verification for pornography. But Plibersek has previously conceded children were easily able to dodge the new rules.
Labor will also soon begin consultation on a digital duty of care bill that will put the onus on tech companies, including AI companies, to make online spaces safer for all users.
Plibersek said the digital duty of care legislation, as well as a second round of privacy reforms, could also help tackle camera-equipped smartglasses, which she said she had serious concerns about.

“Tech companies should know that their products are safe and make them safe before they release them on to an unsuspecting public. I know the Attorney-General has asked the privacy commissioner to look specifically at these glasses,” Plibersek said.

“We’ve got a second tranche of privacy legislation coming up soon as well … things like this that can be used to furtively film, including during sexual encounters, for that filming then to be made public or used against someone who is being filmed as a way of blackmailing them, I am very concerned about the potential uses of these glasses.”

articles.title: LOOK: Kaila Estrada cozies up with Daniel Padilla in Japan trip
articles.summary: Kaila Estrada appears to be more open about her relationship with Daniel Padilla, giving fans a glimpse of their recent Japan getaway with friends. The actress posted on her Instagram a series of…

blocks.text: Kaila Estrada and Daniel Padilla (Instagram)
Kaila Estrada appears to be more open about her relationship with Daniel Padilla, giving fans a glimpse of their recent Japan getaway with friends.
The actress posted on her Instagram a series of photos of them dining at a Japanese restaurant, riding a train, and attending the Summer Sonic Festival with friends.
Kaila and Daniel have not publicly confirmed their relationship, but they have been sharing photos of each other on social media, which fans interpret as proof of their romance.
The two have also been spending time with each other’s families.
In June, Padilla attended the intimate 53rd birthday celebration of Kaila’s father, actor John Estrada.
