articles.title: Dozens of soldiers killed or arrested after an apparent mutiny in Niger's capital, state TV reports
articles.summary: NIAMEY, Niger (AP) — Dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested after a group of young troops attempted a mutiny in Niger's capital in what was seen as a major threat to the country's ruling junta,…

blocks.text: NIAMEY, Niger (AP) — Dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested after a group of young troops attempted a mutiny in Niger's capital in what was seen as a major threat to the country's ruling junta, according to a state television broadcast and analysts.

It was the culmination of nearly 24 hours of unrest that appeared to be staged by young soldiers aggrieved over the worsening militant violence under the country's military junta. Russia's Africa Corps provided aerial and ground support to local forces to resist the rebellion, according to analysts and diplomats.

State broadcaster RTN showed footage of dozens of mostly young soldiers being paraded in public after sustained gunfire and explosions were heard overnight into Saturday at a key military base located within Niamey's main airport and near the presidential palace.
"The fighting lasted a few hours in several places, which allowed (security forces) to gradually control the situation, arrest and incapacitate these moody soldiers," state TV reported.
The whereabouts of military leader Abdourahamane Tchiani were unclear.

Senior Nigerien military officers visited the Africa Corps base at the airport "and expressed gratitude to its servicemen for their assistance in suppressing the rebellion," Russian media quoted Moscow's Ambassador to Niger Viktor Voropayev as saying.

The rebelling soldiers had camped at the military base until late Saturday while the presidential guard secured the presidential palace and was deployed to regain control of the base, analysts and diplomats said.

The loyalist forces have regained the "upper hand at least at the airport (and base)," according to Wassim Nasr, a senior research fellow at the Soufan Center. Some forces were, however, heading to the capital and it remained unclear if they were coming to support the mutiny or the junta, Nasr added.
The Associated Press could not independently confirm whether the Nigerien security forces regained full control of the base.
Unrest started with a hostage situation
Some of the mutinous soldiers came from the southwest of the country, among the regions worst-hit by insecurity, diplomats and analysts said.

The state broadcaster stopped its live transmission for some time on Saturday morning before it resumed. It broadcast a statement from Niger's Defense Minister Gen. Salifou Mody saying a group of soldiers took some officers hostage at the base and shot at "sensitive sites" in a "break with the discipline and military regulations."

The airport is a strategic hub that hosts a Nigerien air force base as well as the headquarters of the joint Niger-Burkina Faso-Mali military force. All three neighbors are now under military rule, following a string of coups in Africa's Sahel region, but are struggling with insecurity.

Niger's junta came to power after a 2023 coup which it said was prompted by the elected government's inability to stem armed violence. Since then, the impoverished West African country of more than 25 million people has severed ties with longtime Western security partners, turning instead to Russia. But the junta has been unable to stem militant violence and rampant killing of security forces, fueling unrest within the military, observers say.

The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, called for unity. "Our Defense and Security Forces are mobilized for the Defense of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive," it said in a Facebook post.

Algeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country has assured Niger, its southeastern neighbor, of its "full solidarity and firm support, with a view to overcoming this ordeal and promoting a rapid return to stability."
Niger's military junta has struggled to stem violence, fueling unrest
It is the third time this year that the base at the Diori Hamani International Airport has been attacked, after two earlier assaults by jihadi rebels.

The attacks are "becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks," said Heni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a conflict monitor.

"Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel, and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fueling unrest within the militaries that seized power," Nsaibia said.
The mutiny adds to pressure on the military authorities, which have been unable to contain deadly jihadi violence.
Before the 2023 coup, Niger had been the West's last reliable partner in the region in battling jihadists linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group in the Sahel.

However, the country's security forces, aided by Russia's Africa Corps, have been overstretched on multiple fronts by jihadi groups whose repeated attacks in the last year have resulted in mass casualties within the military.

articles.title: ‘They’re concrete acts of stewardship’: Cayetano defends Laguna Lakeshore project amid row with Lacson
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano has again defended the Laguna Lakeshore project, highlighting the remarkable progress of the Laguna Lake within the jurisdiction of Taguig City in recent…

blocks.text: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano has again defended the Laguna Lakeshore project, highlighting the remarkable progress of the Laguna Lake within the jurisdiction of Taguig City in recent years and its vast untapped potential.
Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson (Facebook)
Cayetano, in a recent Facebook livestream, also called for better stewardship of God’s creation, as he defended his city’s decision to pursue infrastructure projects within the Lakeshore.

“Nung congressman pa ako ng 1998, naging passion ko na po kung paano pagandahin ang Laguna Lake. Nagkaroon lang po siyempre ako ng opportunity sa side ng Taguig dahil nga ito ang aking home city… Napakarami po kasing gamit ng lake (Back when I was a congressman in 1998, improving Laguna Lake became a passion of mine. Naturally, I had the opportunity to focus on the Taguig side since it is my home city... After all, the lake has so many uses),” Cayetano said in two August 27 live streams along the Taguig Lakeshore.

“Ang pagiging sa gobyerno, ang pagiging public servant — hindi po kami ang may-ari ng resources… Kami po ay stewards, tagapamahala lang. Lahat ng tao kahit na wala sa gobyerno, meron po tayong obligasyon maging good stewards (Being in government, being a public servant—we do not own the resources... We are merely stewards, managers. Everyone, even those outside of government, has an obligation to be good stewards),” he said.

Cayetano related the City of Taguig's lakeshore projects as concrete acts of stewardship, designed to protect the lake from erosion, pollution, and illegal settlements while ensuring public access for all.

“Nung ginawa y’ung C6 or road dike, basically, pinoprotect po y’ung lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only na huwag mag-erode, (but para) hindi bahayan ng informal centers kasi kung mabahayan yung dumi, dito mapupunta sa lawa. The other thing is to make it for public use (When you built the C6 or road dike, basically, you were protecting the lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only to prevent erosion, (but to) not house informal centers because if they were houses, the waste would end up in the lake. The other thing is to make it for public use),” the senator explained.

Cayetano also countered allegations of land-grabbing by pointing out that the local government actually reserved the area for public use, reversing the historical pattern of private encroachment along the lakeshore.

“May allegations na may kinakamkam kami. Hindi ko lang alam kung pag sinabing kami, kung kaming mga Cayetano, kung ako, o kami ng ibang leaders… Doon sa bandang gitna, marami na pong private (land) kasi may 1,100 hectares ng lupa na nasa labas ng road dike. Meron po doon na private property, merong gobyerno (There are allegations that we are appropriating land for ourselves. I am just not sure who is meant by ‘we’—whether it refers to us Cayetanos, just me, or us together with other leaders... In the middle section, there is a lot of private land, as there are 1,100 hectares situated outside the road dike. There are both private properties and government-owned lands there),” he said.

“Pero ito lahat po, precisely ni-reserve at ginawan ng paraan ng local government na maging public para hindi kamkamin. So baliktad sa allegation na kinakamkam. Titingnan niyo po y’ung history. Maraming kumakamkam po ng lupa dito. Pero ang history po ng Cayetano ay tumutulong na maging good stewards para sa gobyerno (But all of this was precisely reserved and secured by the local government for public use to prevent it from being seized by private interests. So, the allegation that it is being grabbed is the exact opposite of the truth. If you look at the history—there are many who do grab land here. But the Cayetanos’ track record shows they help act as good stewards for the government),” he emphasized.

On Saturday, August 29, Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson released further information and identified four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig which he said have been issued fraudulent land titles, while four others lack plotted title lots in the Land Registration Authority’s (LRA) digital file.
Lacson said his public disclosure of the details of the initial findings is to dispel insinuations that his earlier exposes on illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were “fake news.”
“Since Senator Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest,” he said.
In response, Cayetano again, took to Facebook livestream to refute Lacson’s allegations, referring to the former national police chief as a “Marites” and a “Senator-Judge Troll.”
“That senator-judge has been trolling me almost every day. It’s all just gossip, or, as they say, inconclusive, argumentative, and hearsay,” Cayetano said.
“So, if Senator Lacson—our senator-judge-troll—wishes to inspect the developments at the lake, he is most welcome,” he stressed.

articles.title: Canada installs large Lake Ontario sign in latest jab at US
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a billboard on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."

blocks.text: Watch: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils 'Lake Ontario' sign
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has hit back at Donald Trump by installing a large sign on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
The US president signed an executive order on Thursday seeking to change its name to Lake America and has shared a series of AI-generated videos about the lake that straddles both countries.
"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ford said.

The war of words was triggered after trade talks collapsed, with the US imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.
Watch: "He's losing it" - Americans react to Lake Ontario name change
Trump said the decree was effective immediately as he signed the order to rename it Lake America.
While he has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks, other countries are not required to follow. Canadian officials have dismissed Trump's move.
On Saturday, Trump also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, with one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one that says: "Welcome to Lake America."
Another video depicted a flock of Canada geese sporting the US president's hair and holding rifles as they patrolled the shoreline of a newly named Lake America.
Ford said Trump's renaming of the lake was because he "didn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves".

Standing in front of the newly unveiled Lake Ontario sign, Ford added: "Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever."
It echoes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's previous response to the row, insisting "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".

blocks.caption: Map of the Great Lakes region of North America showing Lake Ontario highlighted in red. The map labels Ontario and Quebec in Canada and U.S. states including New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin. The other Great Lakes, Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron,…

blocks.text: The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

When Trump entered the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

articles.title: Going nuts over coco: Discover the Filipino brands reinventing the humble coconut
articles.summary: More than just a fruit, the coconut is deeply woven into the fabric of daily Filipino life. Long revered as the country’s “Tree of Life,” its bark, trunk, leaves, and roots flavor local cuisine,…

blocks.text: More than just a fruit, the coconut is deeply woven into the fabric of daily Filipino life. Long revered as the country’s “Tree of Life,” its bark, trunk, leaves, and roots flavor local cuisine, supply materials for artisanal crafts, and stand today as crucial building blocks in our push toward sustainability and economic growth.

In the Philippines, there is no such thing as “too much” coconut, as local entrepreneurs and creators continue to push the boundaries of what this tree can offer. Reaching beyond food and beverage into beauty, wellness, home essentials, and other sustainable materials, the coconut evolution is proudly showcased at the COCONUTPhilippines Trade Fair 2026.

Convened at the SMX Convention Center in Pasay City, the COCONUTPhilippines Trade Fair 2026, running from Aug. 26 to 30, is the country’s biggest fair yet of the coconut’s modern potential. Featuring over 300 MSMEs, the trade fair was organized by the DTI's Bureau of Market Development, Promotions, and OTOP (DTI-BMDPO), in partnership with the Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA), to empower local enterprises and expand their market reach.
Redefining the Filipino pantry

The SMX Convention Center halls overflowed with unexpected coconut food innovations. While Filipinos have long loved coconut in everything from savory dishes to desserts, it is now making its way onto dining tables as a daily condiment and essential staple.

While coconut vinegar has been around for a while, coconut-based soy sauce and seasonings have featured prominently as amino acid-rich, slightly sweet alternatives to traditional soy sauce. Quezon Province’s Yakap at Halik (YK) Multi-Purpose Cooperative showcased coconut catsup. A blend of coconut milk, water, and vinegar with a milder flavor, perfect for fried and grilled dishes. Marketing staff Teodora O. Glorioso noted DTI’s help in securing certifications to overcome nationwide expansion hurdles.
Coming in hot, MSMEs introduced coconut hot sauces: Hot Heads featured a rich coconut cream sauce infused with habanero, while Quezon’s Best offered a fiery blend from premium chilis.

Finally, The Power of Slow introduced a fresh twist on coconut beverages with a sap-based energy drink. Supporting farmers and wellness, the brand is established overseas, but head of customer development RJ Samson highlighted local adoption challenges, which DTI is actively addressing through trade fairs and mall pop-ups.
Sustainable fashion

Beyond the kitchen, coconut is also making its mark in Filipino fashion. From Zamboanga, Agricooltourist De La Paz (AGL Collection) turns coconut fibers and husks into sturdy yet stylish handbags, an initiative born from the desire to support local farmers, many of whom are also the backbone of their production.
The brand also showcased prototype lamps crafted from the same materials, effectively upcycling agricultural waste from the coconut fruit into functional home décor.

But turning farmers into artisans came with its own hurdles. With limited exposure to the market, the team leaned heavily on DTI for guidance, from labeling and branding to training and seminars covering both handicraft techniques and financial literacy.
With that, Ronnel Barbon, marketing staff, says the brand's next goal is steady growth, securing consistent orders and continuing to refine its products for a wider, more discerning market.
Shells to clean energy
Redefining clean-burning fuel, CG’s Coconut Charcoal Trading of Bohol repurposes discarded coconut shells into charcoal briquettes.

John Mark Baldo, who manages the business operations, shared that the family business stemmed from an unusual romance between his grandparents. What started decades ago as a grandfather's gesture to win over his bride has now grown into an enterprise that manufactures and exports coconut charcoal briquettes to Japan, China, and Malaysia.

As the brand prepares to expand its footprint to additional overseas markets, Baldo emphasized that DTI remains an essential partner in helping them navigate complex international trade regulations, join major trade expositions, and build lasting B2B networks with fellow MSMEs.
Local roots to global reach

Inside the fair, the potential of the coconut continued to unfold across aisle after aisle of organic skincare, personal care products, and eco-friendly home essentials. Yet behind every innovative item on display is a unified government effort to elevate local enterprises. Through joint initiatives, agencies like the DTI and the PCA work hand-in-hand to equip MSMEs with technical guidance, market readiness, and the tools needed to scale for international export.
Further, through SM for MSMEs, Filipino entrepreneurs gain opportunities to connect with customers, build networks, test their products in the market, and open new pathways for growth.

That local traction is already fueling a global impact. Driven in part by this rising wave of commercialized innovations, Philippine coconut exports surged by 34.4 percent in 2025 to reach $3.6 billion, accounting for a vital share of the country's $84.48 billion total export revenues.

With such momentum, the sector is positioned to shape not just the future of agriculture, but the trajectory of the national economy. The coconut remains a testament to Filipino resilience: a resource that sustains rural communities, powers international trade, and anchors a growing culture of innovation. In the Philippines, it seems, there is no limit to what the humble coconut and innovative Filipino minds can do.

Plaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal Fire

A fire in California’s Big Sur region doubled in size overnight, forcing the…

blocks.text: A fire in California’s Big Sur region doubled in size overnight, forcing the evacuation of nearby residents, in a coastal region where firefighters have battled another blaze for weeks.

The Plaskett fire, which sparked on Tuesday, had swept through more than 5,900 acres (2,400 hectares) in Monterey county as of Friday, and remained un-contained, according to Cal Fire. Its cause is under investigation.

blocks.caption: Firefighters watch as the Plaskett fire burns toward Highway 1 on Friday. Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP

blocks.text: Fire authorities have deployed helicopters and air tankers to suppress the flames with targeted water drops, but the remote area’s steep terrain and scarce roads have hindered ground crews’ ability to access the fire.

Meanwhile, to the north, the Timber fire continues to burn through more than 24,000 acres (9,700 acres), as authorities have it under 21% containment. The blaze broke past certain containment lines. Smoke from the fire and cloud cover prevented officials from mapping the fire’s expansion overnight.

blocks.caption: Sage Harvey tosses a rope off the roof of his house as the Plaskett fire approaches on Friday in Big Sur, California. Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP

blocks.text: Both fires have prompted partial closures of Highway 1, whose Big Sur stretch offers a scenic route between Los Angeles and San Francisco.

items: A low pressure area in the Philippine Area of Responsibility has a high chance of developing into a tropical depression named Pilandok.
Tropical Depression Saudel briefly reentered PAR but is not directly affecting the country, while the southwest monsoon is causing rain in various parts of Luzon.

MANILA, Philippines – A low pressure area now inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) has a “high” chance of developing into a tropical depression on Sunday, August 30.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the LPA, located at 1,340 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon, will be called the local name Pilandok once it strengthens.

Meanwhile, Tropical Depression Saudel (formerly referred to as Obet) briefly reentered PAR on Sunday and was located 1,105 km west northwest of extreme Northern Luzon, moving southwestward at 25 kilometers per hour, with maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 75 km/h.
Saudel is not directly affecting the country, according to PAGASA Weather Specialist Obet Badrina.
What is still bringing rain to parts of Luzon is the southwest monsoon or habagat, causing monsoon rain in Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga.

It is also bringing occasional rain to Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro, scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Negros Island Region, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of the Visayas.
Badrina said the LPA could enhance the southwest monsoon again as it moves and strengthens. Below is PAGASA’s latest heavy rainfall outlook due to the southwest monsoon for the next three days:

articles.title: Alan Cayetano wants more details on 2026 spending, gov’t debt as Senate tackles 2027 budget
articles.summary: As the Senate starts deliberations on the 2027 national budget, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano urged the government’s economic team to show how much of the 2026 budget has been spent,…

blocks.text: As the Senate starts deliberations on the 2027 national budget, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano urged the government’s economic team to show how much of the 2026 budget has been spent, where the funds went, and how much the country has borrowed.

In a letter to Senate Finance Committee chief Sen. Joseph Victor “JV” Ejercito, Cayetano raised these questions, saying the information would help senators study the proposed budget and ensure that the budget process is transparent and “faithful to the priorities they all promised to serve.”
“There is no measure this Congress passes each year that is more consequential and touches more Filipino lives than the General Appropriations Act (GAA),” Cayetano said in his letter.
“It is our values and priorities written in numbers. That is why we owe it to our people to get this budget right,” he emphasized.
Earlier, Ejercito kicked off the hearings on the P7.2-trillion national budget during the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) briefing on Thursday, August 27.
Prior to this, Cayetano, in his letter, asked the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) how much of the 2026 budget had been released, committed to projects, and actually paid out.
The senator also called on the DBM to provide each department’s and agency’s absorptive capacity — that is, how much each can realistically spend.

Cayetano also asked whether funds under the government’s Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) framework had reached the intended initiatives, and requested details on their release and use.

The lawmaker also sought details on the national government’s total debt as of July 31, 2026, as well as the loans and bonds it took out or guaranteed over the past three years. He also asked which foreign loans and grants were still awaiting government approval.
Cayetano also requested a list of funds that had been transferred, realigned, or added to other programs since July 2023, including where the money came from and where it went.
He urged the agencies to submit their answers and supporting documents early to provide senators sufficient time to review them ahead of the agency budget hearings.
At the same time, the Minority Leader also assured the Senate Majority bloc of his “full and good faith cooperation” in crafting “the best possible budget for 2027.”
“(It must be) a budget that honors God, builds communities, and transforms the nation,” he said of the proposed 2027 national budget.

articles.title: First Lady bids farewell to outgoing Japanese envoy Endo
articles.summary: First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos held a final catch-up with outgoing Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya and his wife Akiko at her office in Manila, as the couple prepares to wrap up…

blocks.text: First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos held a final catch-up with outgoing Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya and his wife Akiko at her office in Manila, as the couple prepares to wrap up their two-and-a-half-year stay in the country.

In an Instagram post on Saturday evening, Aug. 29, Araneta-Marcos thanked the Endos for their friendship and the memories they made during their stay, saying the Philippines would always be a "second home" to them.
"One last catch-up with Ambassador Endo Kazuya and Madame Endo before they wrap up their stay in the Philippines," the First Lady said.
"Thank you for the friendship, warmth and wonderful memories over the past two and a half years," she added.

The meeting, held in her office at the PMS Building on Aug. 27, featured a light conversation among the three, with the First Lady and the couple seen smiling and laughing in a video posted alongside her message.
The Endos gave Araneta-Marcos a blue Uniqlo polo shirt bearing the embroidered logo of the 70th anniversary of the Philippines-Japan Friendship Anniversary on the left breast.
The First Lady, meanwhile, gave the couple a copy of "Philippine First Ladies Portraits," written by José "Pepe" Rodríguez and painted by artist Lulu "Coching" Rodríguez.
Other keepsakes symbolizing the Philippines were also featured, including a framed map and images depicting traditional Filipino dances such as singkil, tinikling, and cariñosa.
In a Facebook post, Araneta-Marcos said they looked back on the "many special memories" the couple made in the Philippines and, more importantly, the friendships they formed during their stay.
"Thank you both for your warmth, kindness and friendship — and, of course, for the thoughtful gifts!" she said.
“I hope our little keepsakes will always remind you that you have a second home here and many friends who will be happy to welcome you back,” she added.

The farewell came a day after President Marcos honored Endo during a farewell call at Malacañang, conferring on him the Order of Sikatuna, Grand Cross with Distinction, for his contributions to strengthening Philippine-Japan relations.

Endo was recognized for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation in defense, security, and development cooperation, as well as supporting Philippine priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development.

The Presidential Communications Office also cited his efforts to advance Japan's longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including support for the peace process, grassroots development, and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

Endo, who thanked Filipinos in an Aug. 28 social media post as he ended his tour of duty, described his two-and-a-half years in the Philippines as "truly unforgettable" and said he was humbled to have served as ambassador "at the height of our two countries’ partnership."

articles.title: First Lady thanks late Marcos aide-de-camp for ‘courage, loyalty and dedication’
articles.summary: First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos has paid tribute to Maj. Ma. Joshua Santiago, thanking the late soldier for the “courage, loyalty and dedication” with which he served by President Marcos’ side. In an…

blocks.text: First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos has paid tribute to Maj. Ma. Joshua Santiago, thanking the late soldier for the “courage, loyalty and dedication” with which he served by President Marcos’ side.
In an Instagram post late Saturday, Aug. 29, Araneta-Marcos extended her condolences to Santiago’s family, particularly his wife, Argel, and their children, Army and Navy.
“A heartfelt thank you to Major Joshua Santiago for the courage, loyalty and dedication with which he served by my husband’s side,” the First Lady said.
She said the family was in their thoughts and prayers, and assured them that Santiago was deeply valued by those who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him.
“May you find comfort in knowing how deeply Jam was valued, and how much his service, friendship and presence meant to all who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him,” she said.

Araneta-Marcos, who visited the wake at the Libingan ng mga Bayani on Aug. 28, also thanked Santiago for his dedication to duty, saying his service would always be remembered with “respect, gratitude and affection.”

Santiago served as Marcos’ aide-de-camp, a military officer assigned to assist a senior official by handling official engagements, coordinating activities, and providing close support in carrying out the official’s duties.
President Marcos earlier mourned Santiago in a Facebook post, describing him as “a soldier of courage, an officer I could depend on and, above all, a good man.”
The President also visited Santiago’s wake at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Aug. 27, where he was seen expressing his condolences to the family, particularly to Argel.
The video of Marcos’ visit was muted, with only piano music playing, so his conversation with the family was inaudible.
Neither Marcos nor the First Lady mentioned the cause of Santiago’s death.

articles.title: This week’s milestones: Aug. 30 to Sept. 5
articles.summary: Sept. 3, 2006 The National Historical Institute installed a national historical landmark in the Cuartel of Imus in Cavite to commemorate the “Labanan sa Imus.” On Sept. 1, 1896, the forces of Gen.…

blocks.text: The National Historical Institute installed a national historical landmark in the Cuartel of Imus in Cavite to commemorate the “Labanan sa Imus.” On Sept. 1, 1896, the forces of Gen. Emilio Aguinaldo and Col. Jose Tagle attacked the friars and guardia civils who had taken refuge in the Casa Hacienda. The following day, revolutionaries led by Tagle launched another attack while Aguinaldo and his men were fighting in Bacoor. Finally, on Sept. 3, 1896, additional Spanish forces under Gen. Ernesto de Aguirre were defeated. Aguirre’s sable de mando fell during this battle and was captured by the revolutionaries. This victory served as an inspiration to the revolutionaries as they fought for independence.

Calaca was converted from a municipality into a component city of Batangas through a plebiscite, which ratified Republic Act No. 11544, signed by then President Rodrigo Duterte on May 26, 2021. Once a barrio of Balayan situated on the left bank of the Bolbok River, Calaca was established as a town on May 10, 1835. Prior to its conversion to a city, it was already emerging as one of the fastest-growing local economies in Calabarzon and was known as the “Power Town in South Luzon.” Today, Calaca is a third-class city with a population of 92,281, as of the 2024 Census.

The provincial government of La Union and the Baguionas Farmers and Coffee Growers Association (BFCGA) signed a deed of donation for La Union’s first coffee processing facility located in Barangay Libbo, Bagulin. The 78-square-meter facility was funded P2.9 million under Republic Act No. 7171, or the Support for Virginia Tobacco Farmers Act. Construction began on November 18, 2024, and was completed on May 29, 2025. The facility is now operated by BFCGA, whose members are mostly robusta coffee farmers from the indigenous peoples community. Its 33 farmer-members collectively cultivate 30.55 hectares and yield about 400 kilograms of green coffee cherries annually. They supply coffee beans to popular establishments in the surfing town of San Juan.
This week’s festival
Siargao Food and Wine Festival (Aug. 26 to Aug. 31)

The Siargao Food and Wine Festival is the country’s first community-led, island-wide culinary festival that’s taking place in Siargao, Surigao del Norte. In partnership with the Department of Tourism, the festival carries the theme, “Building a Better Island, One Bite at a Time.” It celebrates the people, produce and traditions that shape the island’s food culture through collaborative dining experiences, workshops, markets and community gatherings. The six-day festival offers a series of immersive experiences, including a gala opening on Aug. 26, Ocean Day on Aug. 27, Coconut Day on Aug. 28, Producer Day on Aug. 29 and Community Day on Aug. 30. It will culminate on Aug. 31 with a closing celebration and recognition.
Hadang Festival (Sept. 1 to Sept. 8)

The Hadang Festival is celebrated in Calbayog City, Samar. The festival is named after “Hadang,” which is an ancient ritual dance offering to spirits for blessings such as a good harvest, healing or protection from violence. In 2025, it was declared as the city’s official festival through Ordinance No. 2025-27-658. The ordinance also formally ended the use of the Sarakiki Festival, which had previously been hyphenated with Hadang. This year’s celebration includes a beauty pageant, “Hinadang nga Bulawan, “Uyag Kinahimat-an,” Hadang ritual street dancing competition and grand showdown, concert, fiesta carnival and culminates with the town fiesta on Sept. 8.
Dana Gracielle Quirante, Inquirer Research
