articles.title: A metropolis takes shape around Baguio
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The summer capital has been at the center of a budding metropolis for two years now, although this may not yet be common knowledge. Working behind the scenes is the…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The summer capital has been at the center of a budding metropolis for two years now, although this may not yet be common knowledge.
Working behind the scenes is the fledgling Metropolitan Baguio-La Trinidad-Itogon-Sablan-Tuba-Tublay Development Authority, more commonly known by the acronym BLISTT.

Much like the older Metropolitan Manila Development Authority, the BLISTT metropolis has been quietly examining cross-border problems shared by Baguio and its five closest Benguet neighbors—the provincial capital and vegetable trading center La Trinidad; vegetable-producing towns Tuba, Tublay and Sablan; and Itogon, home to some of the Philippines’ oldest operating mines.

Lawyer Liberato Ramos Jr., one of the authority’s top managers, emphasized that BLISTT would not intervene in the policy directions of individual local governments. Instead, it would serve as a bridge toward joint solutions.
Ramos made the clarification when he introduced the BLISTT Metropolitan Authority for the first time to the Baguio City Council on Aug. 24.
Every local government would have complementary roles in the BLISTT metropolis, according to Marygail Antonette Killa, senior manager for planning and forester Marcial Aloda.
“Baguio City is governance, healthcare, innovation, education, commerce, tourism,” Aloda told the council.
He added: “La Trinidad is focused on agritechnology, education, trade and services. Itogon focuses on ecotourism, watershed, energy and mining.”

“Tuba is a gateway and industrial hub. Sablan is focusing on agri-ecology, rural development, and community and Tublay would (center on) highland agriculture, organic farming, and agro-ecotourism,” Aloda noted.
But while BLISTT intends to concentrate on the urbanizing towns surrounding Baguio, the city remains its “metropolitan core,” Aloda acknowledged.

Problems once shouldered by Baguio alone—overpopulation, excessive waste, dwindling water supplies, traffic gridlock and overconstruction—are now emerging as crises for its Benguet neighbors. Some of these problems have already spilled over from the city.
These issues had been foreseen by the first incarnation of BLISTT as far back as 1990, after the Luzon earthquake once again devastated Baguio.

Conceived and popularized by the late city architect Joseph Alabanza, BLIST—then without Tublay—was envisioned as a blueprint for how Baguio could share or redirect investments and resources to adjoining municipalities to ease the pressure of extreme urbanization.
Affects everyone

blocks.caption: Vincent Cabreza/Contributed photo

blocks.text: Tuba, for instance, could attract investments to develop its rolling hills into suburbs for families working in Baguio, Alabanza said in 1990, when he warned of what he saw as the city’s inevitable societal implosion if it continued along the same path.
More importantly, Alabanza argued that every stage of progress—and the benefits or problems it generates—ultimately affects the rest of BLISTT. Those problems are now here.

When a new comprehensive land use plan was presented to the City Council on Aug. 26, architect Donna Tabangin, Baguio’s planning, development and sustainability officer, said the city built 117 years ago under the American colonial government was closer than ever to the irreversible urban decay projected to occur by 2043.

To slow this grim trajectory, Baguio needs new analytical approaches to problems unique to a mountain city that was designed in 1905 by famed Chicago architect Daniel Burnham as a hill station intended to accommodate no more than 25,000 people.

For instance, Tabangin said the city is now planning around what she calls an “effective population”—not just its residents, but also tourists, students and people from BLISTT and other parts of Luzon who come to Baguio for business.

In 2023, Baguio received 1.3 million tourists. It also had 6,469 nonresident high school students and 22,054 nonresident college students, while 351,833 people came into the city daily for business transactions, according to city data presented by Tabangin.
Baguio’s nighttime population in 2023 was 380,354, but its effective population doubled to 760,708 during the daytime, when consumption of resources is higher.

Baguio now has a clearer picture of how much it needs to conserve after a 2019 urban carrying-capacity study found that key resources and infrastructure, including public roads, forest cover, water and wastewater treatment, were no longer sufficient for its population.
The carrying capacity of Baguio’s roads, based on a standard of 15 square meters per person, was already 218 percent beyond capacity when measured against the resident population, Tabangin said.

“But if you measure the road against an effective population, it really gets worse because we are now 437 percent beyond the capacity,” she added, helping explain the city’s worsening traffic congestion.

“We need a city that’s more compact in such a way that we cannot spread out and encroach more on our open spaces and green spaces because we need that for sustainability. We need to align development with the resource that’s available,” Tabangin said.
Water constraints

blocks.caption: Vincent Cabreza/Contributed photo

blocks.text: Water, Tabangin said, will be the “binding constraint” for all of Baguio’s future programs, business incentives and public service initiatives.
“We are in severe deficit based on computations and it’s rapidly worsening. So development cannot happen if the water supply cannot support the intensity of development there,” she said.
Baguio’s current water deficit stands at 13,900 cubic meters per day, she said, with the city having exceeded its water carrying capacity by 158 percent.
The city’s other life-support systems are similarly under pressure.

Baguio’s forest cover is approaching a “near ecological threshold” and is already 113 percent beyond its carrying capacity, while its green cover, or total vegetation, has a “large capacity deficit,” at 104 percent beyond capacity.
The city’s new land use plan aims to make all 128 barangays more livable, Tabangin said, but doing so requires an audit of Baguio’s living conditions.

Preserving open spaces will be crucial. About 36 percent of Baguio’s 57.5-square-kilometer territory is covered by proclaimed civil and military reservations, equivalent to 2,083.4 hectares (ha), while 3,865 ha are designated as environmental protected areas.
Baguio’s notoriously high land prices are partly a result of these constraints.
Around 2,930 ha are titled properties, while about 658 ha are certified ancestral lands owned by Baguio Ibaloys, including their only ancestral domain.

Tabangin said the new land use plan also seeks to harness Baguio’s demographic dividend, with 70 percent of its working-age population being young and potentially capable of accelerating economic growth.
It has been the city’s youth, she noted, who have often stirred change—from volunteering to clean and repaint school walls to taking up activist causes in the city’s streets. /cb

articles.title: Lacson flags 4 ‘fraudulently’ titled parcels in Taguig
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Four parcels of alleged illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City are covered by “fraudulently” issued titles that will be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman for…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Four parcels of alleged illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City are covered by “fraudulently” issued titles that will be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman for investigation, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Saturday.
In a statement, the senator said he shared the initial findings “to dispel insinuations” that his disclosures regarding the alleged anomalies were “fake news.”
According to Lacson, the parcels covered areas ranging from 5,000 to 193,027 square meters and were processed through various patent and land registration procedures.
He also said there are four other parcels that had no documentation in the Land Registration Authority’s (LRA) digital records.
Lacson said earlier the LRA is examining several titles covering some 38.83 hectares of “illegally” reclaimed areas on the Taguig City side of Laguna Lake.

“I requested the LRA to backtrack the history of the issued OCTs (original certificates of title) and other modes of titling, so we will find out how they were manipulated with the end in view of filing criminal charges against those responsible,” he said in a statement.
He said these titles may be declared “void ab initio” or void from the start, once the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) initiates forfeiture proceedings.
Lacson said the Ombudsman has issued subpoenas to the LRA, PRA, Taguig Registry of Deeds and Department of Public Works and Highways.
“Since [Senator] Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest,” he said in a post on X (formerly Twitter). /cb

articles.title: DENR’s ‘earth-balling’ of mangroves questioned
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — An international environmental group has stepped up calls for the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend its guidelines on the earth-balling or…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — An international environmental group has stepped up calls for the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend its guidelines on the earth-balling or relocation of mangroves, given that their protection is mandated by law.
Amid questions on the legal basis of that activity, the agency is conducting a review, which it said it would complete by early next year.

Oceana Philippines criticized the continued implementation of “Interim Operational Guidelines and Conditions on the Earth-balling and Relocation of Mangroves in Exceptional Circumstances”—a DENR memorandum issued in October last year, which the group said allowed the earth-balling or relocation of mature trees to give way to infrastructure projects.
The group warned further that this activity stripped coastal communities of their first line of defense against the catastrophic impact of flooding and typhoons.

“By allowing earth-balling, the DENR is sacrificing proven nature-based solutions for short-term economic gain,” Oceana vice president Von Hernandez said in a statement on Aug. 28, after Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna appeared at a hearing by the House appropriations committee on Aug. 26.
Cuna explained at the hearing that the DENR, through its research arm Ecosystems Research and Development Bureau (ERDB), has undertaken a review of the earth-balling of mangroves.
He said the study—which is now on its second phase as of August—focuses on the survival rate of mangroves after that procedure.
The DENR will issue a policy report based on the ERDB study by early 2027, he said.
Last month, Mamamayang Liberal Rep. Leila de Lima filed a resolution calling for an inquiry into how the DENR’s interim guidelines would affect the country’s mangroves.
‘Legal validity’

De Lima also sought to establish the “legal validity” of the guidelines, since there are laws mandating the protection of mangroves, as she pointed out—Republic Act No. 8550 (the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998) as amended by RA 10654 and RA 8371 or the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act.

Hernandez, in his group’s statement, had asked: “Shouldn’t the DENR be held accountable for reneging on its mandate to protect mangroves and uphold nature-based safeguards, especially at a time when every coastal community in the country is under siege from flooding and storm surges?” /cb

articles.title: Teodoro: Protecting PH seas a mission for the youth
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — As countries “expand” their claims because of their declining resources, there is a need for the country’s stakeholders, particularly the youth, to protect their resources in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — As countries “expand” their claims because of their declining resources, there is a need for the country’s stakeholders, particularly the youth, to protect their resources in all the country’s waters, not just the West Philippine Sea, the defense chief said in a forum on Saturday.

“As populations expand in the world, as resources grow more scarce, as needs grow more scarce, there is a temptation to expand,” Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. said at the launching of the Bantay Dagat Youth Ambassadors-West Philippine Sea Edition Caravan held in San Juan City.
“And that we cannot allow for your sake in the future,” Teodoro said.

The forum billed “Safeguarding Our Seas: National Duty and Community Leadership in the West Philippine Sea” was organized by the Rotary Club of Chinatown Circle in partnership with the Philippine Navy.
PH waters in Pacific
The Philippines has about 2.4 million square kilometers of maritime domain, Teodoro said, adding that the country’s geography makes the protection of its waters particularly important.

“You cannot stop the growth of human beings, the growth of society,” Teodoro said. “But what you can stop is somebody else taking what should be yours to support yourself and giving it to somebody else.”

He said the Philippines should look beyond the West Philippine Sea when considering its maritime interests, as he cited the Philippine Rise and waters on the country’s Pacific side as potential sources of food and energy for future generations.

“Because all the resources, whether in the West Philippine Sea, in the internal waters, in the Pacific Ocean side of the Philippines, are sources of potential sustenance, energy for future generations,” he said.
Unclos, Hague ruling
Teodoro urged the youth ambassadors to treat maritime awareness as part of a broader effort to strengthen national resilience, including in schools and communities.
“The dimension of how you approach the problem and how you engage the younger generation is multidimensional, because you need to be resilient on land as you do on sea,” Teodoro said.

Teodoro also reiterated the Philippines’ commitment to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) and to the 2016 ruling by the Hague arbitral court in asserting its maritime rights.

China rejects the 2016 ruling on the Philippines’ 2013 arbitral case before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, The Netherlands. The ruling found no legal basis for Beijing’s sweeping claims over much of the South China Sea.
Teodoro said the country is also working to strengthen its ability to defend its maritime domain through military modernization, infrastructure development and security partnerships.

He cited the Philippines’ status of visiting forces agreements with Canada and New Zealand, which he said had entered into force. Another agreement, this time with France, awaits the Senate’s approval, while formal negotiations for a proposed agreement with the United Kingdom have begun, he said. /cb

articles.title: US Department of Agriculture sees surge in PH food insecurity
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is poised to record the highest rate of people experiencing food insecurity in Southeast Asia this year despite a better forecast a decade from now, according to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is poised to record the highest rate of people experiencing food insecurity in Southeast Asia this year despite a better forecast a decade from now, according to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).

The Global Food Assessment (GFA) report of the USDA’s Economic Research Service released Aug. 26 shows the Philippines having an estimated 15.4 million food-insecure people, equivalent to 12.6 percent of its population.
But Indonesia topped the list with 32.1 million food-insecure individuals, representing 11.2 percent of its total population.

The USDA publishes its GFA report annually to assess food demand in 83 low and middle-income countries, including the Philippines. It also monitors each country’s ability to meet this demand from its own production and local sources.
“The resulting gap between local food availability and food demand helps identify potential markets for US agricultural products,” the report said.

The US agency said the Philippines’ per-capita food gap—or the difference between the 2,100 kilocalorie (kcal) threshold and the average calorie availability for food insecure people—is also the most critical at 294 kcal per day. The threshold is the kcal needed for a healthy diet.
Yet despite its continued population growth, the Philippines is expected to reduce its overall rate of food insecurity over the next 10 years due to rising incomes and economic growth, the USDA said.
PH population, GDP forecast
According to the report, the projected number of food-insecure individuals in the country will decline to 5.7 million by 2036 or 4.1 percent of the population.
The Philippine population is anticipated to reach 138.7 million by 2036, a 13.8-percent increase from 121.9 million in 2026. This reflects an annual growth rate of 1.3 percent.
Still, the country’s food gap is seen to narrow to 243 kcal per day over the decade.
The USDA also estimated the Philippines’ gross domestic product (GDP) to reach $789.49 billion, surging by 85.5 percent from $425.63 billion in 2026.
Moreover, the report noted that the per-capita GDP is projected to reach $5,691 in 2036 from $3,899 in 2026.

On a regional basis, USDA said Southeast Asia will exhibit the most significant improvement in food security within Asia, expecting a reduction of 72.4 percent in the number of food-insecure individuals between 2026 and 2036.
“By 2036, only 2.5 percent of the population in this subregion is projected to be food insecure, compared to 9.9 percent in 2026,” the report said. /cb

articles.title: UN, Nepal warn of climate threat after deadly floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s foreign minister and the U.N. climate chief on Saturday warned of the growing threat from global warming to the Himalayas, as rescuers race to find thousands of people…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s foreign minister and the U.N. climate chief on Saturday warned of the growing threat from global warming to the Himalayas, as rescuers race to find thousands of people missing after torrential flooding along the border with China.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the disaster on Wednesday near the high-altitude border was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a torrent of debris downstream, with nearly 3,000 people missing and 682 confirmed dead.
While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he had spoken by phone with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, and agreed to increase the sharing of “real-time hydrological data,” according to a statement.

Wang, in a Chinese Foreign Ministry statement, said Beijing had “shared crucial information with Nepal, including disaster area imagery, satellite and hydrological data, as well as early warnings about upstream barrier lakes.”
Wang added that “China and Nepal are bound by mountains and rivers, sharing a common destiny.”

Khanal earlier told reporters that Nepal needed more research to “understand the changing dynamics of the Himalayan ecosystem” and the risks they pose to the landlocked country, encircled by India and China.
That includes not only risks “to Nepal and the downstream community, but also to our northern neighbor, China, as well,” Khanal said.
Himalayan glaciers, which provide critical water to nearly 2 billion people, are melting faster as the planet heats, exposing communities to unpredictable, costly disasters.
Khanal said climate change required international action.

“We always highlight that Nepal contributes less than or just about 0.01 percent of greenhouse gases but we, the people of Nepal, are one of the major victims of the changing climate and its impact,” he added.
“So we request the global community also to come together to preserve the Himalayan ecosystem.”
U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell, meanwhile, said in a statement that the “sudden glacial collapse and flash flood are a devastating reminder of how fragile these mountain environments can be.” /das

“We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe, with vulnerable communities often hardest hit,” he added.
Melting glaciers and thawing permafrost can also destabilize mountain slopes, increasing the risk of landslides and other hazards.

articles.title: Groups want P80 tax on vapes
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A group of health advocates urges lawmakers to impose a tax of P80 or higher on vape products, saying that current government proposals are insufficient to prevent access and…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A group of health advocates urges lawmakers to impose a tax of P80 or higher on vape products, saying that current government proposals are insufficient to prevent access and addiction.

In a statement, lead convenor Jaime Galvez Tan of the Health Philippines Alliance (HPA) said: “The proliferation of these products has accelerated the early onset of chronic heart and lung diseases among our youth.”

“Allowing young people to develop chronic health conditions early in life guarantees staggering medical costs for our healthcare system down the line. Hence, taxing these products at P80 or higher is an indispensable preventive health measure,” said Tan, former health secretary.
Unified tax
The group noted that the Department of Finance and the Department of Health had earlier proposed a unified tax of P72.93 by 2027 for cigarettes, heated tobacco products and vape products.
But it argued this tax rate “remains insufficient to curb access and prevent addiction,” adding that “weak tax rates endanger Filipino youth and place a heavy burden on our healthcare system.”

HealthJustice Philippines, a member group of the alliance, also rejected a proposal to lower taxes on vapes to P15 per milliliter, describing it as “a veiled attempt of the tobacco and vape industry to introduce more addictive products to our youth and hook them to long-term addiction.”

“We cannot allow lower tax rates that enable more addictive substances, like nicotine salt vapes, to proliferate in the market,” said lawyer Benedict Nisperos, legal consultant of HealthJustice Philippines.

He said eight countries of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations have already imposed a total ban on vape products, while the Philippines “continues to allow the sale of these addicting and health harming products.”
‘Predatory marketing’

“Slashing tax rates further, paired with an already lenient Vape Regulation Law [or Republic Act No. 11900], effectively invites more predatory marketing aimed straight at young Filipinos,” Nisperos said.

In an earlier statement, the House committee on ways and means said it is studying proposals to adopt a unified excise tax rate for salt nicotine and freebase nicotine products, with the goal of addressing disparities that may influence consumer behavior and cause market distortions.
Cagayan de Oro Rep. Rufus Rodriguez had proposed a unified excise tax of P15 per milliliter during a hearing on Aug. 25.
He noted the importance of setting a rate that raises revenue without driving consumers toward illicit products. /cb

articles.title: Norway’s King Haakon VIII pays tribute to late father in first speech
articles.summary: OSLO — Norway’s new King Haakon VIII on Saturday addressed Norwegians for the first time since taking the throne, paying tribute to his 89-year-old father, who died the day before. “Above…

blocks.text: OSLO — Norway’s new King Haakon VIII on Saturday addressed Norwegians for the first time since taking the throne, paying tribute to his 89-year-old father, who died the day before.
“Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties,” Haakon said of the late King Harald V in a televised speech.
The new regent said it had been “deeply moving to see all the people, candles, messages and flowers filling up the Palace Square.”
“We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us,” the 53-year-old said.
Visibly moved, he also noted that his father and mother, Queen Sonja, would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.
“Happy anniversary, dearest mamma,” he said, choking back tears.

Flags flew at half-staff on Saturday as scores of Norwegians continued to flock to the palace, adding flowers to the masses already on the ground after more than 20,000 people paid their respects Friday.
The late king enjoyed massive support, despite the slew of scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign.
‘My turn’
Haakon thanked his father for being such “a wonderful papa” to him and his sister Märtha Louise, and acknowledged that “a huge task awaits me.”
“He reminded our family constantly that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own path forward. Be ourselves,” Haakon said of his father.
“Now it is my turn,” he declared.
Kari Lyngestad, a 45-year-old nurse, said she was moved by what she described as a very “emotional” speech.
“I’m happy and I’m sad, and I believe everything is going to be OK. We have a good new king,” she told AFP outside the palace just after the broadcast.
Meanwhile, teacher Eyvind Storeheier called it a “fantastic” speech.
“I think he will be much like his father. He will be a king of the people,” the 56-year-old said.
Tributes have poured in from European monarchies and world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, who hailed the memory of “a strong, proud, and greatly respected man.”
Earlier Saturday, King Haakon held audiences at the palace with the leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and Supreme Court.
He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre for a viewing of the late king’s casket, which was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital Friday evening.
Memorial services Sunday
A national period of mourning has been declared. No date has been set for the late king’s funeral.
Churches across the country will hold memorial services on Sunday. The royal family was scheduled to attend a service in Asker, south of Oslo.
On Tuesday, King Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament.
City halls across Norway set out condolence books on Saturday for the public to write personal messages.
Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who had called off her own wedding on Friday due to the king’s death, was the first to write a message in Oslo’s City Hall.
“Dear King Harald, you didn’t need a crown to be a king. Thank you so much for everything you have done for our city. We will never forget you,” she told reporters she had written.
King Haakon and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, are not expected to be crowned in a ceremony — Norway abolished coronations in 1908.
But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.
King Harald was widely seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway, and praised for leading a monarchy that was modern and modest.
Scandals

Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since Aug. 17, suffering from hemolytic anemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule.
The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family. Queen Sonja, also 89, was herself briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems.
Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, is under scrutiny for her ties to the late U.S. sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
And in June, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing.
Mette-Marit, 53, who suffers from a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July. /das

articles.title: Ombudsman: Courts have been ‘too forgiving’ of graft convicts
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines— The Supreme Court should “police the judiciary” and look into cases of individuals convicted of graft who have been able to post bail at the discretion of lower courts, Ombudsman…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines— The Supreme Court should “police the judiciary” and look into cases of individuals convicted of graft who have been able to post bail at the discretion of lower courts, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said on Saturday.
Remulla made the statement on the same day the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) announced the opening for the position of Chief Justice.
The former justice secretary was frustrated with how the Sandiganbayan and regional trial courts (RTCs) have been handling graft and corruption cases that could drag on for years, even decades.

“The problem is courts are too forgiving that they do not imprison those that should be imprisoned,” Remulla stressed in his weekly radio show, “Executive Session,” on dzRH. “If you have been convicted by a lower court, convicted by the Sandiganbayan, convicted by the RTC for graft, you should already be in prison.”
“Hopefully the Supreme Court, of course they are our friends, should police the judiciary properly. They should really monitor [the cases] and set deadlines,” he added.

Under the Rules of Court, being admitted to bail even after conviction of graft or violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act that are not punishable by reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment is subject to the trial court’s discretion.
Remulla stressed that courts are too lenient when it comes to such cases even when those found guilty already lost “presumption of innocence” and their right to bail.
Search for new chief justice
He said if they push through with the rules on allowing bail, the grant should be steep and should be set at the cost of damage committed by the convicted person.

Remulla noted that his office is already working on an inventory showing the status of individuals sentenced to prison upon conviction of graft—whether they indeed went to prison or they were able to escape serving time because they were granted bail.
But he said that it is still up to the courts, especially the Supreme Court, on how to properly implement bail rules and how to expedite resolution of cases.

The JBC said it would be accepting until Oct. 13 this year applications and recommendations for the new top magistrate who will succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who is set to retire on Nov. 6.

Gesmundo became the 27th chief justice of the Supreme Court in April 2021, a little over a year before President Rodrigo Duterte finished his term. He was a Sandiganbayan justice before Duterte appointed him to the high tribunal as associate justice in 2017.
Next to him by seniority is Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, who was appointed to the Supreme Court in 2010 by then President Benigno Aquino III.
Of the current 15 high court justices, including Gesmundo, only Leonen and Justice Alfredo Caguioa were appointees of Aquino; and only Justice Raul Villanueva was appointed by President Marcos.
The rest were appointed by Duterte, including Justice Filomena Singh, who was appointed at the eleventh hour, just a month before the ex-President stepped down in June 2022. /cb

articles.title: ‘Demand high’: 500 patients awaiting kidney donors
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Human Organ Preservation Effort of the National Kidney and Transplant Institute (HOPE-NKTI) is encouraging the public to become organ donors for the more than 500…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Human Organ Preservation Effort of the National Kidney and Transplant Institute (HOPE-NKTI) is encouraging the public to become organ donors for the more than 500 individuals in the country currently in need of a transplant.
According to Dr. Anthony Russel Villanueva, head of HOPE-NKTI, the average number of deceased organ donors in the hospital is “not increasing,” with only around 10 to 12 per year.
On the other hand, he said, there are now more than 500 patients in need of an organ transplant, based on the NKTI data from 2025.
Villanueva also reported that the hospital attended to 64,000 new dialysis patients in 2024.
The number of dialysis patients tend to increase by around 10 percent to 15 percent each year, with most of them qualifying for a kidney transplant, he added.
Culture factor
“The demand is high but the number of our organ donors is low, so we really need the help of everyone for advocacy. So that it would be in our culture to donate,” Villanueva told reporters on Friday.
“In other countries, it’s a great honor for them to donate. When you become an organ donor, you are a hero to the community. Hopefully we can have that same mindset,” he added.
To become an organ donor, the public can sign up by scanning the QR code that can be accessed through the HOPE-NKTI’s official Facebook page.

Villanueva explained that HOPE-NKTI deals with deceased organ donations, which involves patients who have already been declared as “brain dead.” Aside from organs, he said, bones and tissues, including corneas, can also be donated to help not just those with illnesses but also persons with disabilities.
One challenge
But before any organ can be donated, consent must be secured first from the family of the potential donor, he stressed, adding:
“By our experience, even if it’s in your license that you are an organ donor, we still need the consent of the legal next of kin.”

Villanueva acknowledged that obtaining such consent can be challenging. “Because we are (usually) an extended family, sometimes a sibling has already agreed but they want to wait for their sister’s or mother’s [agreement].”

“When it takes time, that is a challenge because of the viability of the organ. From brain death, there will come a time where the heart stops, and by then [the organ] is no longer viable for donation,” he explained.
To prevent this problem, Villanueva urged those who are planning to become organ donors to speak with their family regarding their decision.
“They are really the ones who decide. Maybe you consented in your personal [capacity], but of course, the family’s [consent] is still needed,” he said. /cb

articles.title: Ontario premier answers Trump’s ‘Lake America’ with ‘Lake Ontario’ sign
articles.summary: TORONTO — Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as…

blocks.text: TORONTO — Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage.

Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford unveiled the sign near Grimsby, Ontario, and posed for photographs. The 24-by-12-foot (7.3-by-3.6-meter) sign stands on 6-foot (1.8-meter) legs, putting its top about 18 feet (5.5 meters) above the ground — roughly two stories high. The message is repeated in French, one

The display followed Trump’s executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” After months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state and personal attacks on its leaders, the reaction in Canada has mixed defiance with mockery.
Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves” and argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
Canadians mock Trump
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.

“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump’s executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.
“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.
But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”
Canada and the US trade barbs over collapsed talks

The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.

Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”

Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.

Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.
Ontario name has Indigenous origins

The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.
“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name. /das

articles.title: Trump cannot deport students for criticizing Israel, judge rules
articles.summary: SAN JOSE, Calif. — Citing the importance of the First Amendment, a federal judge in California says the U.S. government is unconstitutionally silencing critics of Israel’s war in Gaza and…

blocks.text: SAN JOSE, Calif. — Citing the importance of the First Amendment, a federal judge in California says the U.S. government is unconstitutionally silencing critics of Israel’s war in Gaza and others as part of the Trump administration’s quest to deport noncitizens who it says disrupted college campuses while expressing their views.

Judge Noël Wise, in a ruling Friday, delivered a victory for The Stanford Daily, the student newspaper at Stanford University, which has said some international students were afraid to speak out because of the deportation threat.
“Freedom of speech is illusory if we are only ‘free’ to express complementary views about the government and its leaders,” the judge wrote.

The decision largely piggybacks on findings from nearly a year ago by a U.S. district judge in Boston, who ruled that the Trump administration violated the Constitution when it targeted people who are not citizens for deportation solely for supporting Palestinians and criticizing Israel.

Wise wrote that the freedoms of speech and the press are “foundational to America’s enduring democracy.” The judge cited free-speech and vagueness flaws that violate the First Amendment and Fifth Amendment as she struck down portions of the provisions that the federal government follows regarding deportations.

Wise cited retaliation in March 2025 by U.S. immigration authorities against people who engaged in speech supporting the Palestinians and against Israel’s actions — which a growing number of experts, including those commissioned by a U.N. body, have said amount to genocide. The judge also cited retaliation against people who were critical of Charlie Kirk after the Turning Point USA co-founder was assassinated last September.

“Tomorrow, or perhaps even today, targets may include anyone in the United States who exercises their freedom of speech to simply express opinions the government does not like,” the judge in San Jose said.

“This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognizes our right to speak freely,” she added. “Here you can simultaneously hate the content of a person’s speech and love the country that cherishes the freedom to allow it. Zealous protection of our Constitutional right to free speech is a provocative demonstration of our country’s powerful lack of fear.”
The Justice Department did not respond Saturday to a message seeking comment on the decision.

George Porteous, the editor-in-chief of The Stanford Daily, responded to the ruling by saying on X: “The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation. Today’s victory means they won’t have to.”
Conor Fitzpatrick, an attorney with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which brought the lawsuit, praised the ruling.
“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” Fitzpatrick said in a release.
In her decision, Wise said it was clear that the government’s tactics have had an effect on college campuses.

“The government has offered a chilling message regarding protected speech — speak out against Israel or in support of Palestinians and we will revoke your visa and deport you. Behave. Noncitizen students heard the warning and heeded. And, as the idiom goes, the silence is deafening,” the judge wrote.

At The Stanford Daily, lawfully present noncitizens at the paper have quit, withheld articles, refused assignments, requested articles be taken down, and asked for anonymity due to fear of adverse immigration consequences, Wise noted.
She said noncitizens have the same First Amendment rights as citizens and yet were left to guess what the U.S. foreign policy was at any given moment and on any given subject.

“This is an incomprehensible standard,” she said. “While the Court understands that the government has been granted considerable discretion on foreign policy and immigration matters, that discretion must nevertheless still ensure that ordinary people can understand what the law permits and prohibits.”

Wise added: “Our Constitutional right to freedom of speech guarantees people the right to express — through their words, actions, or assembly — opinions that may be repugnant, views that run counter to prevailing political norms, or beliefs that otherwise challenge the country’s domestic or foreign policy, military engagement, or war.” /das

articles.title: Weeks of Luzon flooding, landslides kill over 30
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Floods and landslides triggered by monsoon rains and enhanced by four weather disturbances so far this month have left more than 30 people dead, mostly in Luzon, authorities…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Floods and landslides triggered by monsoon rains and enhanced by four weather disturbances so far this month have left more than 30 people dead, mostly in Luzon, authorities said.
Nine Aetas in Zambales and Pampanga and two workers at Subic Bay Freeport were among the latest fatalities confirmed on Saturday.

A lahar warning was also issued on Saturday for communities in Pampanga, where the devastation of the 1991 Mt. Pinatubo eruption remains indelible in local memory. This time, however, the threat of “noneruption lahar” is not due to volcanic activity but to heavy rains letting deposits of pyroclastic material loose on local rivers.
A section of the decades-old Aquino Bridge in Tarlac province collapsed Friday night. Public works officials traced the cause of the structural damage to the strong currents of Tarlac River.
This month alone saw four tropical cyclones entering the Philippine area of responsibility, with the latest, Typhoon Obet,(international name: Saudel), being the 15th for the year.
In August 2025, the country by then had experienced only the ninth cyclone of the year, Isang (Kajiki).
Benguet landslides

blocks.caption: LIFELINE A rescue operation on Friday in a neighborhood in Cabangan town in Zambales, one of the areas in Luzon that has been pummeled by heavy monsoon rains this month. —Photo from Cabangan MDRRMO

blocks.text: The Office of Civil Defense (OCD) on Saturday placed the death toll due to weather-induced calamities at 32, starting the count from “Luis” (Peilou) which made landfall on Aug. 3. After Luis was “Maymay” (Kujiri) on Aug. 5 and “Neneng” (Gaenari) on Aug. 18 but no landfall and “Obet” on Aug 24, also no landfall.
At least 8 million people, or 2.3 million families, have been affected across 10 regions, the OCD said.
Among provinces, Benguet recorded the highest number of deaths with 15, all from landslides. Ten of them were in Baguio City, three in Atok town and two in La Trinidad.
Four deaths were recorded in Rizal province, with two of them due to a rockslide in Rodriguez town. One person was pinned to death by a fallen tree in Antipolo, while another drowned in Binangonan.
Batangas province recorded four deaths: one drowned in Batangas City and another in Mabini, one was electrocuted in Lipa, and another was killed in a landslide in Santa Teresita.
The other fatalities were recorded in the provinces of La Union, Quezon, Oriental Mindoro, Occidental Mindoro, and Negros Occidental, and in Caloocan City.
At least 19 people have been injured, including 12 in Benguet province.
Three people remained missing: one each in Quezon City, Manila and Batangas City.
Infra, agri damage

blocks.caption: In Tarlac City, the middle portion of Aquino Bridge, which connects to several towns in Tarlac and Mangatarem,Pangasinan, collapsed before midnight on Friday

blocks.text: The affected regions as of Saturday were Regions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 9, as well as the Cordillera Administrative Region, Calabarzon, the National Capital Region and Mimaropa (Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan).
Some 25,800 people from 7,500 families were staying in 297 evacuation centers.
The OCD said about 2,900 houses had been damaged, including 349 classified as totally damaged.
Damage to infrastructure was estimated at P6.11 billion, while agricultural losses were placed at P2.32 billion.
At least 117 local government units have declared a state of calamity, with the government releasing P1.65 billion worth of relief assistance, the OCD added.

Communities along the river systems draining Mt. Pinatubo were placed on heightened alert around 11 a.m. on Saturday, after the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) warned that heavy rains could generate noneruption lahars.
Aeta passengers

blocks.caption: Weeks of Luzon flooding, landslides kill over 30

blocks.text: Major rivers on the western side of Mt. Pinatubo still hold significant deposits from the volcano’s 1991 pyroclastic density currents, mainly mixtures of ash and rock fragments.

The potential lahar flow is likely to be confined to the upper to middle reaches of the Sto. Tomas-Marella and Bucao river systems, but could turn into muddy streamflows and flooding downstream, affecting communities in San Marcelino, San Narciso, San Felipe and Botolan.
They are among the river systems covered by a government dredging project that has been going on for the last six years.
Nine members of Aeta communities, including five children, have died in two separate incidents in Zambales and Pampanga.

In Zambales, recovered on Saturday were the bodies of two children, age 3 and 8, who went missing after a boat carrying 13 Aeta passengers capsized on Wednesday in Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino town.
The search was still ongoing at press time for the last missing passenger, a 26-year-old pregnant woman.
In Pampanga, a 73-year-old Aeta man died in a landslide at Barangay Pidpid in Porac town on Friday, according to Vice Gov. Dennis Pineda.
The landslide occurred about 20 kilometers south of Mt. Pinatubo amid persistent rains.
Pineda said at least 30 Aeta families had been relocated to the Pio evacuation center near the Porac town proper as a precaution.
Subic incident
At the Subic Bay Freeport, two people died and two others were injured after being buried in a landslide at Tipo High-Tech Park on Saturday.

Initial reports from the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) Law Enforcement Department identified the dead as Peng Jiahan, 26, a Chinese national and a sales and marketing supervisor at Fubong Environmental Technology; and Ernesto Ramos, a Filipino dump truck driver.
Details regarding the two injured victims were still being verified as of press time.
Earlier, the SBMA reported that a “soil erosion incident” occurred at Tipo due to nonstop heavy rains. —WITH REPORTS FROM MADELLE MADAYAG, PHILIPPINE NEWS AGENCY

image.caption: Merkel said with so much attention on the AfD, some voters do not know what other German parties stand forImage: Annette Riedl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: August 30, 2026
Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.
Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.

"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.

Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.
But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.
"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.

‘My heart goes out to all the Nepalese families who are grieving loved ones,’ Cara Severino says. Follow latest updates live

An Australian woman, Cara Severino, who was…

blocks.text: Missing Australian woman Cara Severino found after Nepal floods
Cara Severino, an Australian woman in Nepal who was missing following devastated floods, has been located and is in contact with officials, Penny Wong’s office has confirmed.

The foreign minister’s office confirmed overnight Severino was travelling to a safe location with the help of Australia’s consular officials, who travelled by four-wheel-drive to Kathmandu to locate her along a trekking route.
Wong, the foreign minister, said:

double quotation markThis is a rare piece of positive news amid a disaster that has brought immense loss and uncertainty … I have spoken directly with her and am very pleased to know she is safe. She has also spoken with her family, which I know will be a great relief to them. While this is a welcome development, there remain grave concerns for the other Australians who are still unaccounted for, given the tremendous scale of the flooding and its impact.
Australian consular officials are working with local authorities to find and help those affected by the disaster including Australians who remain unaccounted for, Wong said.
