articles.title: Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’
articles.summary: Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley council

blocks.text: A Sydney library has returned to its borrowing shelves a book critical of Israel called How to Sell a Genocide following a public campaign and an intervention from the State Library of New South Wales.
Waverley library removed the book “for review” earlier this month after the Jewish news outlet JWire reported it had approached the council.

JWire said a survivor of December’s antisemitic attack at Bondi, during which 15 people were killed, saw How to Sell a Genocide on the “new release / hot item” shelf and wrote on Facebook that the display was distressing for survivors and bereaved families.
Guardian Australia was unable to locate the Facebook post. Waverley library at Bondi Junction is in the same council area as Bondi beach.
A staff member at the council-operated library on Friday confirmed the book was back on its shelves. Waverley council was contacted for comment.

The State Library had written to the council reminding it of its obligations under guidelines issued by the Library Council of NSW and the Library Act “which was amended in 2026 to reinforce their independence to develop and maintain collections”.
“The State Library of NSW supports free and equitable access to information,” a spokesperson said.

“The library acknowledges that some books and materials may not align with everyone’s personal views, experiences or beliefs, but supports the right of individuals to make their own choices about what they read, view and access.
“The library has outlined to Waverley council the law and policy relevant to this situation.”

Ramia Abdo Sultan, a lawyer, helped organise a change.org petition calling for the book to be returned to the shelves. She said in a social media post on Thursday that Waverley library’s manager had notified staff that was happening.
“There are 21 people so far queued up in a waiting list for that book,” Abdo Sultan, a board member of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, said.
The petition to restore the book was signed by almost 2,500 people.
“We acknowledge and respect the grief and trauma experienced by victims of violence and antisemitism,” it stated.

“However, individual distress, offence or political disagreement should not determine what the broader public is permitted to access through a public library. Readers should be afforded the opportunity to access books freely and form their own opinions on the contents of the book.”
The book, published by Pluto Press and written by Adam Johnson, critiques what it claims is the US media’s “complicity in the destruction of Gaza”.

Johnson welcomed the decision to reinstate his book but criticised the council for “thus far refusing to answer what complaint prompted the book’s removal”. Johnson said he hoped to find out “through legal channels”.
“It’s obviously a good development the council decided to end their ban of the book amid pressure from free speech and Palestine activists, whose support I am grateful for,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“But it was never about one library or one book, but about the increased suppression of pro-Palestine speech in Australia, which has radically escalated over the past seven months. Attempts to blame Palestine solidarity and sympathies for the Bondi attack, as the book ban advocates repeatedly did, is the real story. This false and sleazy conflation must stop.”
Guardian Australia approached the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (Ecaj) and the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies for comment.
Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive officer of Ecaj, previously welcomed the book’s removal.
“A book of this sort has no place on the shelves of a library, especially one within minutes of where Australians were slaughtered [at Bondi],” Ryvchin told the Sydney Morning Herald.
“I commend the individual who spotted the book, herself a survivor of the massacre, and acted to have it removed.”
Bart Shteinman, an executive member of the progressive Jewish Council of Australia, said the book should “never have been removed in the first place”.

“This debacle should be a lesson for other councils that stifling literary freedom only confuses and undermines the critical struggle against antisemitism and all forms of racism,” he said on Thursday.
“Banning books is not something any council should be doing.”

The president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, Nasser Mashni, said: “That a single complaint was enough to trigger the removal of a book about the genocide in Palestine should concern every Australian who values free inquiry and open debate. These efforts must be resisted.”

Multiple human rights groups have said Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, which Israel denies. In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry found Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

At the time the book was removed, a Waverley council spokesperson said: “The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection.”

articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
articles.summary:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor…

blocks.text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.
Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

blocks.caption: Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”
It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Protests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya. Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”
The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.
That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: Protesters set fire to migrant camp in Ceuta
articles.summary: The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.

image.caption: Police had to intervene when protesters began setting fire to the parts of the campImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRES/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and clashed with police on Thursday. The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
Footage on Spanish television showed a group of demonstrators on a beach, throwing objects into the fire. Police pushed the protesters back while the migrants retreated to a pier.
Earlier on Thursday, a military vehicle was attacked with stones and other objects by about 70 people, a police spokesman in Ceuta told the AFP news agency.
Local protesters tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from reaching the beach to distribute food to migrants. People waving Spanish flags shouted "They should leave" and "Out with the Red Cross."

blocks.caption: Locals in Ceuta accuse the government of mishandling the situationImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: How many migrants are still in Ceuta?
In July, more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly in the hope of reaching the European mainland.
While the vast majority of them have since returned to Morocco, several thousand remain in Ceuta, living on the streets or on the beach.
Spain's government in Madrid puts the number at below 7,000 while Ceuta officials say it's at least 10,000. Ceuta's population is about 84,000 people.
Growing pressure on Madrid

The Spanish government is under growing pressure over the situation in Ceuta. The conservative opposition is accusing left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to act and abandoning Ceuta's residents.

Madrid has recently moved to speed up efforts to identify the migrants and decide who will be sent back to Morocco. The government also approved extra funding to help unaccompanied minors entitled to special protection.
The crisis comes ahead of general elections next year and has deepened political divisions in Spain. The conservative opposition is calling for a tougher stance on migration.
The mass influx in July had also led to tension within the EU over how to respond to the situation in Ceuta.

articles.title: Days after deadly Nepal flood, families of missing B.C. couples desperate for details

blocks.text: British Columbia
Days after a massive wall of water tore through the Timure region of Nepal, families of two missing Metro Vancouver couples are desperately searching for information about their loved ones.
Federal officials say 32 Canadians still missing
Families of Canadians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood cling to hope

Port Moody couple Dhaval and Megha Shah and Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing since the Aug. 26 flash flood struck, killing at least 570 people.
Vikram Khosla said his cousin Shubakshi was in the area for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, as a 50th birthday gift to herself.
Nepal-Tibet flash flood death toll climbs as fears of 2nd flood grow
He said the couple had been almost ready to depart for their journey when they spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck on Wednesday morning.
No one has heard from anyone in the group since then, he said.
“We are very hopeful that they went up and they are stuck somewhere," he said.
The couple, Singaporean citizens who moved to Canada about four years ago, have two daughters, he said.
Speaking from Mumbai, India, Dhaval's brother Kheval Shah told CBC his brother and sister-in-law were staying at Hotel Kailash, near the border, on Wednesday.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: The family last heard from the two that morning as they were having breakfast, about 15 minutes before the flood struck.
“That hotel is completely submerged, there is no hotel anymore," he said.
“We just want to find out where they were when the water hit.... Ultimately I feel that closure is very important.”
The couple have a 24-year-old daughter, he added.
Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
CBC News Network speaks to extreme weather researcher about Nepal/Tibet.
But Shah said he wants the Canadian government to push Nepal for more information about the search for the missing.
Khosla, too, shared frustration with the lack of updates.
He said Shubakshi's brother and sister have flown to Kathmandu and are trying to get to the affected area to search for answers.
He wants to see a centralized source of information for the families of missing people to get real time updates.
As of Saturday, about 3,000 people remained missing in the disaster.
No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued.
With files from Georgie Smyth, Tanya Fletcher and The Canadian Press

articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
articles.summary:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release…

blocks.text: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.
Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.
Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.
The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.
Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’
articles.summary:
President denies visit was to gain support for Iran sanctions or due to fears that Putin plans to ‘test Nato resolve’

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by the Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.

Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.
“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.
“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.

“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.

The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year. Trump’s efforts to end the war – which he once vowed to bring to a conclusion on “day one” of his second presidency – have proven unsuccessful, despite his friendly personal relations with Putin.
Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin during his visit.
after newsletter promotion

Washington and Moscow have found themselves on opposite sides following Trump’s decision last February to go to war with Iran, with Russian satellite technology said to have been used to help Iranian forces with precise targeting of US and allied bases in the Gulf and beyond.

With military hostilities at an impasse, the US treasury department this week unveiled a new program of economic warfare against the Tehran regime involving secondary sanctions against countries that trade with it. To be effective, it would need the cooperation of allies of Iran such as Russia and China, experts say.
Peskov did not give a reason for Ratcliffe’s visit, but described forecasts that it would lead to an upturn in US-Russian relations as “premature”, the Washington Post reported.

“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive phenomenon, a positive process. These contacts often continue even in the most difficult moments of bilateral relations,” Peskov told reporters. “But whether this will affect, on the whole, the process of bringing our bilateral relations out of the deep crisis they are in – it’s premature to say at this point.”
In recent days, Ukraine has targeted Russia’s energy infrastructure and online retail facilities in long-distance strikes, while Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Kyiv.

articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
articles.summary:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents…

blocks.text: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment

blocks.text: The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

articles.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
articles.summary:
The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected

A fresh outbreak of mpox

blocks.text: A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.
What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

blocks.caption: A colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.
Why is it spreading to new countries?
There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

blocks.caption: A Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPA

blocks.text: In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.
What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

blocks.caption: A passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India. Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFP

blocks.text: The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.
How worrying is the new outbreak?
Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”

blocks.caption: Furaha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC. Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/Reuters

blocks.text: However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”
Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.
Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

blocks.caption: A young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPA

blocks.text: An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”

articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive
articles.summary:
Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost

As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza, and Julian Borger

blocks.text: As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.

With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.

Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.

“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.

blocks.caption: Yousef at work in 2024. He was killed by a drone-fired missile that year aged 24. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”

Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.
The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.

Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.
“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee works on his plants nursery in Gaza

blocks.text: Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.

He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.

“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.”

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee checks the state of crops grown for the production of seeds. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Increased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, but according to UN agencies there are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse.

Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production.
“Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee harvesting aubergines. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Based on satellite data, the FAO estimates that little more than a quarter of Gaza’s total prewar cropland, 4,100 hectares, remains accessible, and only about 3%, 450 hectares, is undamaged, free of debris and ready for immediate cultivation.
Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army has pushed the “yellow line” steadily forward over the course of the ceasefire.

Using specialised satellite imagery, the human rights advocacy group Forensic Architecture carried out a survey of flora across Gaza as a measurable proxy for cultivable land. It found that nearly 68% of the territory’s flora was on the Israeli side of the yellow line and another 5% was inside a buffer zone declared by the army, delineated on maps with an orange line, where it is extremely dangerous for Palestinians to venture.

Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, was shot dead along with another man when they came within range of Israeli sniper positions. Their bodies were left out in the open for two days because it was too dangerous for their relatives to retrieve them.

The family’s old farm is now under Israeli control, so after the ceasefire was declared they came to Beit Lahiya to try to start again from scratch on leased land. Since last October the army has pushed the yellow line forward, swallowing up nearby farms in west Beit Lahiya.

“The expansion has had a devastating impact on the agricultural sector,” Abu Rabee said. “Fertile farmland that farmers had worked tirelessly to cultivate after spending everything they had or even borrowing money, simply it was seized just as it was ready for harvest, leaving them with nothing.”

blocks.caption: Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, who was shot dead in July. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: On the remaining land, the challenges appear endless. With hardly any livestock left, there is little homegrown dung-based fertiliser, so the family are improvising by piling decaying vegetation under tarpaulins. Meanwhile, they are battling nematodes and other soil infestations and a chronic lack of water, all the time under the constant, unpredictable threat of death.

Abu Rabee said: “Stray bullets frequently reach this area and strike many places around us. Many people have also been wounded in the streets as a result of indiscriminate attacks. I fear for my own life simply because I’m a farmer.”

articles.title: Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdown
articles.summary:
As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime

Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign…

blocks.text: Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.

For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.

Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.

“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.

Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.

blocks.caption: The Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery, who was sentenced in absentia to 15 years in prison for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran.  Photograph: Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle/Polaris/eyevine

blocks.text: Although Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s 12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.

Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regime protests that led to thousands being killed in January.

She came to international prominence in 2019 after criticising Trump’s use of one of her photos of a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.
Now, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.

“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.
Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.

“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.
“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” she said.

blocks.caption: Casualties in Tehran of an airstrike during the 40-day US-Israeli war on Iran, taken by Yalda Moaiery on 15 March. Photograph: Yalda Moaiery/Reuters

blocks.text: Moaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.
“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”
She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei.

“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”

articles.title: In Ohio, Canada-U.S. trade war sparks anger and uncertainty

image.caption: Joe Koch’s construction company has been in operation since the 1980s. He says he feels caught in the middle of the trade war between Canada and the U.S. (James Young/CBC)

blocks.text: The rat-a-tat-tat of a nail gun and high-pitched whine of a buzz saw echo through the two-storey home as Joe Koch’s carpentry crew completes the final touches.

Koch, the vice-president of operations for his decades-old family business, had hoped there would be three or four other new builds going up in this Ohio subdivision about now, but the U.S. trade war with Canada and many other countries has scuttled that plan.

"People are just going to not build that house this year. They're going to wait 'til interest rates lower. They're going to wait 'til the tariffs subside or the political landscape changes," Koch said.

He sees his business challenges as a microcosm of what’s happening across Ohio. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canadian and other nations' goods have not only raised the prices he pays but costs for consumers more broadly.

items: One of Trump's top deputies has been unsatisfied with trade deal on the table for Canada, sources say
Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'

blocks.text: Koch used to buy Canadian shingles. Now he buys from a local company.
"If there's any benefit [to the trade turmoil], it's that you get that much more resourceful," he said.

The uncertainty and instability of the trade war has made financial planning and supply management difficult. Koch believes when it comes to trade, building relationships and making compromises is important.

"When it comes to the real volatile landscape of the globe, you need partners within your backyard that you're able to go to," he said. "I think it may be great to be able to have everything homegrown — but is that the reality of the world? I'm not so sure."
Koch feels caught in the middle of a trade storm but he’s determined to tough it out.

"It's a game of chess," he said. "There's no victory. It's just battle after battle and you win where you can. You try to minimize the damage wherever there is damage. And then you live to fight another day."
"But we're used to it," he said. "We're Youngstown, Ohio."
'It makes me angry'

Youngstown/Warren, which has a population of around 425,000, has faced economic challenges before. It was once known as the heart of U.S. steel country, until the closure of Youngstown Sheet and Tube in September 1977 put 5,000 workers out of work overnight.

While Youngstown diversified its economy in the decades that followed, more than 20,000 jobs are still tied to manufacturing, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That's across numerous sectors, including steel tubes and pipes, plastics and advanced materials.
‘Nonsensical’: We asked Americans what they think about the trade war

Last year, Ohio exported $17.5 billion US in goods to Canada — roughly a third of its total exports. Ohio’s top exports to Canada included $2.7 billion US in engines and turbines, $1.8 billion in auto parts, $1 billion in plastics and $692 million in iron and steel alloys and semi-finished products, according to data from the Embassy of Canada in Washington, D.C.

Conversely, Ohio imported $3.2 billion US in Canadian crude oil, $1.1 billion in vehicle parts, $1 billion in plastics, $915 million in steel and semi-finished products, and $672 million in aluminum and aluminum materials.
Youngstown sits in a wider congressional district known as OH-6 with a population of more than 775,000.
It exports more than $820 million US in goods to Canada every year, including coal and petroleum, iron steel and ferroalloys, resins and synthetic fibres, aluminum products and plastics.
While not all of these imports and exports are caught in the crosshairs of the escalating tariffs, a prolonged trade war could threaten some businesses in those sectors.
What Canadian goods is Trump targeting with his latest 50% tariffs?

At a local ballpark recently, players were hanging out for a post-game beer in the parking lot under the glow of a warm sunset. But there were also heated words about the Trump administration's trade war with Canada.
“It makes me angry. Why is that? Because, first of all, Canada and us have been very good allies forever, and to do something like this makes no sense at all," said Pam Hall. "It's just ridiculous.”
Next to her, Patricia Vandervoort chimed in: “We don't want Canada to hold it against us citizens — it's not us.”
Hall said the administration’s trade war with Canada and other countries is hitting Ohioans in the pocketbook.

“Everything you buy is more expensive, no matter where it comes from, because of these tariffs. Groceries, basic day-to-day items that you need,” she said. “The tariffs have … done a lot to destroy the economy.”
Their friend Cindy Burns fears Canada may permanently take its business elsewhere.

“I'm sure you're going to strengthen trade with other countries to supplement what we're not giving you or trading with you. You'll go elsewhere and maybe it'll be better and you'll never come back,” Burns said.
“It'll affect our factories, because there won't be a demand that there has been. People will lose their jobs. I mean, it's gonna spiral,” said Vandervoort, a Pennsylvania native.
Not far away, Larry Kelly believes the tariff war could flip seats blue in this red state in the November midterms.

Some polling in the Buckeye state has shown Democrats competitive and even ahead in some key races, including for a Senate seat currently held by Republican John Husted, who was appointed by the Republican governor to replace now Vice-President JD Vance.
“I think it's going to have a dramatic effect on the midterms," said Kelly.
His teammate Mike Glinatsis says the trade war hasn’t affected him that much.
“I mean, I can afford to eat,” he said. “I think Canada had … high tariffs on our stuff. And then Trump made it equal. And that's when people started getting all pissy.”
Tariffs 'a mixed bag'
Others in the business community share Glinatsis’s more positive view of the tariff war.

“There's a mixed bag — it hurts some, it helps some. And there's some companies where it hurts on one side, it helps on the other," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber.
One of the major steel companies in town is in favour of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, Coviello said.

“Sometimes in those meetings, I've got a chamber member that is trying to argue against tariffs sitting across the table from a chamber member that's embracing the tariffs, and it is interesting to hear them talk it out.”
Companies and agriculture producers in Ohio are still trying to figure out how the Canadian counter-tariffs, set to begin on Sept. 8, will affect them.
Coviello said data from Youngstown State University’s Export Assistance Network suggests overall, the trade war has been a “net negative.”
Americans 'rethinking who truly has their back'

The trade war has stymied growth potential for some Ohio businesses, such as Shapes Unlimited, which fabricates aluminum gates, fences and other materials. It employs roughly 40 people in the Youngstown/Warren area and has just moved into a new facility with major investments in technology.

"We'd like to further extend our reach into the provinces, but it isn't cost-effective right now,” said CEO Doug Rende, who has been eyeing markets in Ontario and Quebec, given their proximity to northeastern Ohio.
“The issues associated with transportation surcharges, rising fuel costs and obviously the 50 per cent issues associated with tariffs make it untenable.”
Rende’s business has had to work hard to source aluminum amid the tariff war, with levies ranging from 25 to 50 per cent on imported aluminum and an elevated demand for domestic and scrap supply.
“You can't cut off your nose to spite your face until such time as you're finding ways to more aggressively invest in the capacity,” Rende said.

The U.S. did once make more of its own raw materials, he said.

“This country abandoned investments in aluminum manufacturing in the 1980s, where there were 30 smelters. Now there's four. So again, [the government's] fire-ready-aim approach is unnecessarily raising costs to the end consumer, making housing costs less [affordable], and certainly negatively impacting by millions of dollars our ability to be more profitable in utilizing this material on an ongoing basis.”
Rende said he’d like to buy Canadian aluminum because of its quality and its proximity to Ohio, which would help significantly shorten the lag time in its supply chain.
Rende’s patience with the trade war is growing thin.

“Regardless of the political affiliations and points of view of your prime minister and our president, the bottom line is it's affecting us as individuals, as consumers, it's affecting us as businesses and business owners, and it's driving up issues that can be easily averted,” he said.
He believes this spat and its knock-on effects will play a role in how Americans vote in November.
“I think the U.S. population is now rethinking who truly has their back — and we'll see.”
